High‑temperature tensile tests (up to 1400 °C) reveal a pronounced increase in hardness correlated with the volume fraction of the fine Nb₃Ta phase; specimens with >12 vol % Nb₃Ta exhibit hardness values that rise by ≈30 % relative to samples with <5 vol % precipitates, while the larger ZrW₂ particles contribute little to strength due to their incoherent interfaces. The observed hardening is attributed to effective precipitation strengthening and impediment of dislocation glide, whereas the coarse phase merely acts as a weak link, slightly lowering yield strength at elevated temperatures. These findings underscore the importance of controlling precipitate size and distribution in tailoring the high‑temperature mechanical response of NbTaZrWCr.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: the effect of secondary phase or precipitate content on hardness

text: WCrVZrTiNb was fabricated by arc melting under an argon atmosphere, with each ingot remelted at least four times to ensure chemical homogeneity. The resulting alloy was then drop‑cast into a steel mold and subsequently subjected to a rapid quench, producing a fine equiaxed microstructure with an average grain size below 50 µm. Optical microscopy revealed a homogeneous distribution of a solid solution matrix, with no detectable intermetallic precipitates. Compared to Ni‑based superalloys, the refractory HEA exhibits a markedly higher lattice distortion due to the wide atomic radius spread among W, Cr, V, Zr, Ti, and Nb, which enhances solid‑solution strengthening and suppresses dislocation glide at temperatures above 900 °C. Mechanical testing in a high‑temperature compression setup showed a relatively flat flow stress curve up to 1100 °C, indicating superior thermal stability. The absence of gamma‑prime or carbides, which dominate high‑temperature creep resistance in Ni superalloys, suggests that the refractory HEA relies on its intrinsic solid‑solution strengthening and grain‑size‑controlled creep mechanisms for maintaining strength, offering a promising alternative for extreme‑temperature applications.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: comparison with conventional Ni-based superalloys in high-temperature contexts
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: In TaHfWReMoNb fabricated by powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering, the as‑sintered microstructure typically comprises a fine, nearly equiaxed solid solution with occasional Re‑rich secondary particles. During subsequent thermal exposure, the lattice distortion introduced by the wide size mismatch among Ta, Hf, W, Re, Mo, and Nb acts as a strong impediment to dislocation glide, yet it also elevates the driving force for recrystallization. Consequently, nucleation of strain‑free grains initiates at the high‑energy grain boundaries and pre‑existing Re‑rich particles, leading to a rapid reduction in stored energy. The recrystallized grains subsequently grow, but their rate is moderated by the high melting temperatures and low diffusion coefficients of the constituent elements. Grain growth follows a parabolic law, with the growth exponent slightly reduced in comparison to conventional FCC alloys because the multicomponent solid solution suppresses vacancy mobility. Thus, the material reaches a stable grain size that balances the reduction in defect density with the preservation of the fine‑grained microstructure necessary for superior strength.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: recrystallization behavior and grain growth kinetics

text: The refractory high entropy alloy TaMoHfRe is synthesized by first mechanically alloying equiatomic elemental powders, a process that drives the system toward a single-phase solid solution through severe plastic deformation and local mixing. Thermodynamically, the mixing enthalpy of this composition is modestly negative, reflecting the similar sizes of the constituent elements and the comparable electronegativities, which collectively favor the formation of a disordered face‑centered cubic lattice. The valence electron concentration (VEC) for TaMoHfRe is close to 4.5, placing it near the boundary between body‑centered cubic and face‑centered cubic stability ranges; thus, the solid solution adopts an fcc structure at room temperature. During hot pressing, the high processing temperatures suppress the formation of intermetallic compounds, while the retained compositional entropy stabilizes the single phase. Consequently, the alloy’s thermodynamic parameters promote a uniform microstructure with minimal secondary phase precipitation, which is critical for achieving the desired high-temperature mechanical performance.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: thermodynamic considerations (mixing enthalpy, valence electron concentration)

text: Arc‐melted and subsequently drop‐cast NbTaCrZrTiVMo alloys were examined to elucidate the temperature evolution of their tensile response. Microstructural analysis revealed a predominantly body‑centered cubic (BCC) matrix with minor intermetallic precipitates of TiCr and ZrMo; grain size remained fine (~2–3 µm) after casting. Instrumented indentation indicated that hardness and elastic modulus decline progressively with increasing temperature, reflecting lattice softening and reduced interstitial constraint. Tensile tests performed between 25 °C and 900 °C showed that both yield strength and ultimate tensile strength follow a similar trend, dropping markedly above 600 °C, consistent with the disappearance of the solid‑solution strengthening effect as solute atoms become increasingly mobile. The measured hardness values correlate closely with the elastic modulus, supporting the notion that both metrics are governed by the same underlying lattice stiffness and grain boundary strengthening mechanisms, which are progressively weakened as temperature rises.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: temperature dependence of tensile strength and yield strength

text: In the ZrReTiNbWHf refractory high‑entropy alloy, the high lattice distortion from the large size mismatch between Zr, Re, Ti, Nb, W, and Hf creates a sluggish diffusion environment that limits the formation of coarse intermetallics during laser additive manufacturing. However, the rapid solidification inherent to directed energy deposition can trap hydrogen in interstitial sites, especially near the high‑entropy matrix and at residual porosity. Hydrogen preferentially accumulates at grain boundaries and in any Ti‑rich precipitates that may form during post‑processing, promoting local embrittlement through the formation of brittle hydrides or by enhancing decohesion at the interface between the alloy matrix and secondary phases. The presence of Hf and Nb, which possess lower hydrogen solubility, tends to localize hydrogen in the Zr–Re–Ti–W network, creating stress concentrations that reduce fracture toughness and elongation. Consequently, controlling the residual gas environment, employing post‑processing heat treatments that drive hydrogen out, and refining the microstructure to minimize porosity are critical for mitigating environmental embrittlement in this material.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: environmental embrittlement and hydrogen effects
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Suction casting of the two refractory high‑entropy alloys, TiWNbZrTa and VTiWCr, in an argon‑purged environment yields dense, equiaxed microstructures with modest porosity. In TiWNbZrTa, the constituent elements generate a large lattice distortion due to the mismatch between the relatively small Ti and Zr atoms and the much larger W, Nb, and Ta atoms. This distortion promotes strong solid‑solution strengthening, while the presence of Zr stabilizes a body‑centered cubic matrix that retains higher dislocation mobility at elevated temperatures. The combination of a relatively fine grain size (~10–15 µm) and pronounced lattice distortion leads to a higher hardness that, according to Tabor’s relation, should translate into a correspondingly elevated yield strength. Conversely, VTiWCr, although also possessing a high‑entropy composition, experiences a less pronounced lattice distortion because Cr and V have atomic radii closer to the mean. Its microstructure is dominated by a more coarse, mixed BCC/HEX phase distribution and a slightly larger average grain size (~20–25 µm), resulting in lower hardness and, therefore, a lower yield strength relative to TiWNbZrTa.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: the qualitative correlation between hardness and yield strength (Tabor-type reasoning)

text: In a series of tensile experiments on HfNbCrZrVMoW fabricated by directed energy deposition, extensometer data reveal a clear Hall‑Petch correlation between average columnar grain dimensions and mechanical response. Samples exhibiting finer, sub‑5‑µm grains—achieved by optimizing laser power and scanning speed—display increased yield strength and Vickers hardness relative to their coarser‑grained counterparts, which typically feature 10–20‑µm columns. The elongated grain structure promotes higher dislocation storage and reduced cross‑grain slip, leading to elevated resistance against plastic deformation. Consequently, elongation at fracture is modest for the fine‑grained material, reflecting a trade‑off between strength and ductility. Conversely, specimens with larger grains show slightly higher true strain to failure but lower hardness, indicating a weaker Hall‑Petch effect due to decreased grain boundary density. These observations underscore the critical role of micro‑scale grain refinement in tailoring the strength–hardness balance of this high‑entropy alloy.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: the relationship between grain size and both strength and hardness (Hall-Petch-type reasoning)

text: Samples of the refractory high entropy alloy MoNbTiWVRe were fabricated by vacuum induction melting, employing a 15 kW induction coil in a 99.999 % pure Ar atmosphere. The ingots were repeatedly melted and turned to homogenize the distribution of the five constituent elements, followed by a 5 h soak at 2100 °C and furnace‑cooling to 800 °C to promote the formation of a single β‑phase matrix with a network of intermetallic precipitates. Optical and SEM imaging revealed that as the Re content was increased relative to the other elements, the volume fraction of fine TiMo₂‑type intermetallic particles grew, while the average grain size of the β‑phase decreased. Micro‑hardness measurements displayed a monotonic increase in Vickers hardness with higher secondary phase content, consistent with the strengthening effect of fine coherent precipitates and the impediment of grain boundary motion. Conversely, samples with lower Re concentrations exhibited coarser grains and a sparse precipitate population, leading to comparatively lower hardness values. The observed hardness trends underscore the critical role of controlled secondary phase precipitation in tailoring the mechanical performance of MoNbTiWVRe alloys.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Powder blends of Ti, V, W, Mo, Re, Ta, and Cr (nominal equiatomic composition) were fabricated by high‑energy ball‑milling for 12 h under argon, then cold‑sintered via spark plasma sintering at 1800 °C under 60 MPa for 5 min to achieve >95 % theoretical density. The resulting microstructure exhibited a homogeneous bcc solid solution with occasional Cr‑rich Laves‑phase precipitates (<5 vol %) and a fine equiaxed grain size (~2 µm). Elastic modulus was measured by resonant ultrasound spectroscopy, yielding a value near 400 GPa, markedly higher than in binary Ti–W alloys, indicative of strengthened metallic bonding driven by the high valence electron concentration and substantial lattice distortion from the disparate atomic radii. Cyclic loading on notched bar specimens, applied at 10⁶ cycles per second with a strain amplitude of 0.1 %, revealed a fatigue limit that increased with applied load frequency, suggesting that the dense solid solution and limited crack‑growth pathways from the fine grains confer resistance to crack initiation. The observed correlation between the high modulus, pronounced bonding character, and improved fatigue endurance underscores the role of compositional tuning in refractory HEAs.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: elastic (Young's) modulus trends and their relation to bonding character and composition
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy VWZr (V–W–Zr) produces a dense BCC matrix in which the large atomic size mismatch between V (111 pm), W (139 pm) and Zr (160 pm) generates substantial lattice distortion. This distortion promotes strong solid‑solution hardening, raising the elastic modulus and reducing ductility relative to monometallic BCC constituents. In such brittle systems, notch sensitivity is governed primarily by the ability of the material to nucleate and propagate microcracks ahead of a stress concentrator. The high dislocation resistance and limited slip systems of the BCC lattice suppress plastic blunting around a notch tip, so stress concentrations remain sharp and microcrack initiation occurs at comparatively low applied loads. Consequently, the fracture toughness of VWZr is markedly reduced in the presence of notches, as the critical stress intensity factor for crack propagation is lowered. Microstructural features such as finer grain size or the deliberate introduction of coherent secondary phases can mitigate notch sensitivity by providing additional crack‑deflection pathways or by promoting localized plasticity at the notch tip, thereby enhancing the overall fracture toughness of the brittle BCC alloy.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrTaCr, fabricated by laser‑directed energy deposition, exhibits a markedly different high‑temperature response compared to conventional Ni‑based superalloys. Its near‑equiatomic composition generates pronounced lattice distortion, which impedes dislocation glide and enhances high‑temperature yield strength beyond that of typical γ‑phase Ni alloys, while avoiding the severe γ′ precipitation required for superalloys. The presence of a dense, ultrafine columnar microstructure—formed by rapid solidification and subsequent solution treatment—provides a high grain‑boundary density that refines the effective creep activation volume, reducing creep strain rates at elevated temperatures. Moreover, ZrTaCr demonstrates superior thermal stability, as the solid solution remains single‑phase up to temperatures where Ni‑based systems begin to lose γ′ coherency. However, the alloy’s susceptibility to intergranular corrosion under oxidizing environments remains a limitation absent in Ni‑based matrices. Overall, ZrTaCr offers a promising high‑temperature platform with enhanced strength–temperature performance relative to conventional Ni superalloys, contingent upon improved oxidation resistance.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: comparison with conventional Ni-based superalloys in high-temperature contexts

text: Laser additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloy WMoHfTiZr by directed energy deposition produced columnar microstructures with pronounced porosity and residual stress gradients. In situ resonant ultrasound spectroscopy measured the bulk elastic modulus of as‑built parts, revealing a modest reduction relative to fully dense samples, attributable to the presence of micro‑voids and incomplete fusion zones. Mechanical testing demonstrated that fracture toughness decreased sharply when porosity exceeded 1.5 vol % because stress concentrators localized crack initiation at pore sites, while fatigue life collapsed beyond 0.5 vol % porosity due to accelerated crack propagation through defect‑rich pathways. Conversely, specimens exhibiting less than 0.5 vol % porosity maintained crack‑toughening mechanisms associated with the high lattice distortion of the WMoHfTiZr matrix, preserving superior fatigue endurance. These findings underscore the critical importance of controlling processing defects to harness the intrinsic toughening capabilities of this high‑entropy system.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: the effect of porosity or processing defects on fracture toughness and fatigue performance

text: MoHfZrVCrNbW, fabricated by powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS), exhibits fracture toughness values that improve markedly when the microstructure is dominated by a single solid solution phase with a fine, equiaxed grain network. During SPS, rapid heating and short dwell times suppress the precipitation of brittle intermetallics such as Mo₂V and HfCr, thereby maintaining a high fraction of the BCC solid solution. This promotes a dense array of high‑angle grain boundaries that can deflect propagating cracks, increasing the critical stress intensity factor. Conversely, the emergence of secondary Ti‑rich or Hf‑rich lamellae during extended sintering introduces planar interfaces that act as preferred crack initiation sites, reducing toughness. Moreover, the spacing of any remaining precipitates is found to be crucial; finer spacing facilitates crack bridging, whereas coarser spacing permits easier crack propagation. Consequently, controlling phase purity and optimizing grain boundary character through precise SPS parameters directly governs the observed fracture toughness trend in this refractory high‑entropy alloy.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: fracture toughness trends and their relation to phase content, grain boundary character, and crack path

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy NbWCrTiRe was performed at 2100 °C inside an argon‑purged chamber to suppress oxidation and maintain stoichiometry. The molten alloy, held in a quartz mold, was rapidly drawn into the mold by a controlled vacuum, yielding a near‑fully dense ingot with minimal porosity. Following casting, the sample was solution‑treated at 1900 °C for 2 h to homogenize the solid solution and then furnace‑cooled to 1200 °C before slow cooling to room temperature, promoting a fine equiaxed microstructure. Hardness mapping via Vickers indentation revealed a uniform distribution of hardness values around 500 HV, consistent with a single, highly distorted body‑centered cubic phase. Mechanical testing showed that the yield strength measured in compression closely followed the Tabor relation, with a ratio of yield strength to hardness near 3:1, confirming that the hardness is a reliable proxy for the alloy’s yield resistance. This correlation underscores the role of solid‑solution strengthening and grain‑size control in governing both hardness and yield strength in NbWCrTiRe.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: the qualitative correlation between hardness and yield strength (Tabor-type reasoning)
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Powder‑metallurgical synthesis and spark plasma sintering (SPS) were employed to fabricate the refractory high‑entropy alloy NbZrMoVTa. The as‑sintered microstructure consists of a single BCC solid solution interspersed with nanometric intergranular secondary phases of Nb‑rich and Zr‑rich composition, reflecting the strong lattice distortion imposed by the five‑component system. Subsequent annealing at 1800 °C for 24 h in vacuum promotes extensive homogenization: the BCC matrix becomes compositionally uniform, grain boundaries become cleaner, and the volume fraction of intergranular precipitates diminishes. Transmission electron microscopy reveals that the annealed alloy exhibits markedly reduced lattice strain and fewer dislocation pile‑ups, indicative of relieved internal stresses. These microstructural changes translate into a more stable mechanical response: the hardness stabilizes at a higher plateau, and tensile tests show a slight reduction in yield strength but a notable increase in ductility, consistent with the lower density of heterogeneous interfaces and the increased grain size. Overall, homogenization heat treatment optimizes the balance between strength and plasticity in NbZrMoVTa by refining the microstructure and mitigating micro‑stress concentrations.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure

text: A thermodynamic framework was applied to evaluate the high‑entropy alloy TiVCrTa fabricated by laser additive manufacturing via directed energy deposition. The constituent elements exhibit near‑zero average mixing enthalpies, indicating a propensity for a single solid solution phase rather than intermetallic segregation at the high processing temperatures characteristic of laser deposition. Valence electron concentration (VEC) falls within the range that stabilizes the body‑centered cubic lattice, which is corroborated by in‑situ X‑ray diffraction during rapid solidification. The calculated parameter ΔHmix is close to zero, while the atomic size mismatch, quantified through the σ parameter, remains moderate, suggesting that solid‑solution strengthening will dominate over precipitation hardening mechanisms. These thermodynamic indicators predict a homogenous microstructure with suppressed intermetallic formation, potentially yielding isotropic mechanical behavior and high formability in the as‑printed condition.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: thermodynamic considerations (mixing enthalpy, valence electron concentration)

text: Arc‐melting of the stoichiometric CrHfMoReTiTaV feedstock in a water‑cooled copper crucible produced ingots with an almost homogeneous melt; subsequent drop casting into a preheated copper mold yielded rapid solidification with a pronounced columnar dendritic microstructure elongated along the casting direction. X‑ray diffraction and electron backscatter diffraction revealed a strong basal‑plane texture, with {0001} planes preferentially oriented parallel to the casting axis, indicating directional solidification as the dominant texture‑forming mechanism. Standard tensile specimens (ASTM E8) machined parallel and perpendicular to the casting axis displayed markedly different mechanical responses: the longitudinal specimens exhibited higher ultimate tensile strength and lower yield strength, while the transverse specimens showed the opposite trend, suggesting anisotropic hardening behavior. Transmission electron microscopy of the fractured surfaces revealed dislocation pile‑ups concentrated at grain boundaries perpendicular to the tensile axis, whereas longitudinal specimens displayed more uniform slip bands, consistent with the observed anisotropy. The observed directional differences are attributed to the interplay between the columnar grain structure, basal‑plane texture, and the resulting variation in active slip systems during deformation.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: In a laser‐directed energy deposition experiment, a MoReZrCrTi alloy powder (composition 20 at.% each) was processed into cylindrical specimens with a 1.0 mm wall thickness. The laser parameters were set to a power density of 2.5 kW cm⁻² and a scan speed of 800 mm s⁻¹, resulting in a rapid solidification rate of approximately 10⁶ K s⁻¹. Post‑processing, the samples were solution‑annealed at 1900 °C for 2 h and water‑quenched to preserve a single β‑phase matrix with fine equiaxed grains (~5 µm). Tensile tests were performed at strain rates ranging from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻¹ s⁻¹. At the lowest strain rate, the material exhibited the lowest yield stress but a pronounced work hardening behavior, while at the highest strain rate, yield stress increased markedly and the hardening rate decreased, indicating a strong strain‑rate sensitivity driven by lattice distortion and limited dislocation mobility. The observed trend correlates with the high atomic‑size mismatch among Mo, Re, Zr, Cr, and Ti, which promotes a high intrinsic strain‑rate sensitivity in this refractory high‑entropy system.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: strain rate sensitivity of strength properties
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: The comparative microstructural assessment of HfTiWZrTa and HfTiReVW, both fabricated by arc melting and subsequent drop casting, indicates that the latter alloy is likely to exhibit higher elongation at fracture. In HfTiWZrTa, the constituent transition metals generate a pronounced lattice distortion that promotes solid‑solution strengthening but also favors the formation of a dense, coarse body‑centered cubic network of (Hf, Zr, Ta) rich precipitates. These coarse intermetallics act as preferential sites for crack initiation under tensile loading, constraining ductility. Conversely, the inclusion of Re and V in HfTiReVW introduces a more uniform distribution of fine, coherent (Hf, V, Ta) precipitates and a slight increase in the solubility of Ti, which collectively reduce internal stress concentrations. The finer precipitate spacing in HfTiReVW allows for greater strain partitioning between matrix and precipitates, enhancing plastic deformation before failure. Thus, microstructural homogeneity and precipitate refinement in HfTiReVW favor greater elongation at fracture relative to HfTiWZrTa.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy NbWMo in an argon‑protected environment yields a dense, single‑phase microstructure with fine equiaxed grains that are further refined by the rapid solidification inherent to the process. Instrumented indentation on polished surfaces reveals a hardness that increases monotonically as the testing temperature is reduced, with the elastic modulus remaining comparatively temperature‑stable, suggesting that lattice vibrational contributions dominate the modulus while dislocation activity governs hardness. Tensile tests conducted over a wide temperature range corroborate this trend: the yield strength rises sharply at cryogenic temperatures, reaching a plateau that is only slightly lower than the room‑temperature value, whereas the ultimate tensile strength exhibits a pronounced decrease with increasing temperature, reflecting the activation of thermally assisted slip systems in the bcc‑like lattice of NbWMo. The correlation between indentation‑derived hardness and tensile yield strength underscores the role of grain‑size‑limited solid‑solution strengthening, while the temperature sensitivity of ultimate strength points to the diminishing effectiveness of the high‑lattice‑distortion environment at elevated temperatures.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: temperature dependence of tensile strength and yield strength

text: In a recent study of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ReHfZrTiTaCr fabricated by powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering, the influence of secondary phases on hardness was examined through systematic elongation measurements performed with an extensometer during tensile testing. The microstructural analysis revealed the presence of fine, coherent carbides and a minor Re‑rich intermetallic precipitate dispersed within the solid solution matrix. These precipitates, with spacing on the sub‑micron scale, imposed local lattice distortions and impeded dislocation glide, thereby elevating the material’s hardness. Simultaneously, the extensometer data indicated a reduced true strain to fracture compared to a matrix‑only counterpart, suggesting that the precipitate population contributes to strain‑rate sensitivity and limits plastic flow. The correlation between increased precipitate fraction, higher measured hardness, and lower elongation at fracture supports the view that controlled precipitation can enhance strength at the expense of ductility in this high‑entropy system.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: the effect of secondary phase or precipitate content on hardness

text: In TaMoZrTiWV alloys fabricated by vacuum induction melting and subsequently processed by additive manufacturing, the thermomechanical history imposes a pronounced crystallographic texture. During layer‑by‑layer deposition the rapid solidification and directional heat extraction align the dominant {110} planes along the build axis, while the {111} family remains preferentially oriented perpendicular to the build direction. When such a textured sample is subjected to high‑temperature tensile testing in a controlled‑atmosphere furnace, the load path relative to the underlying texture governs the measured strength. Specimens pulled parallel to the build direction experience a higher effective shear resistance because the primary slip systems lie oblique to the loading axis, yielding elevated ultimate tensile strength and reduced ductility. Conversely, specimens loaded perpendicular to the build direction exhibit lower yield stress but greater elongation, as the active slip systems align more favorably with the applied load. This anisotropy underscores the importance of microstructural alignment in dictating the mechanical response of refractory high‑entropy alloys at elevated temperatures.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples

text: Powder‑metallurgy synthesis followed by spark‑plasma sintering of the refractory high‑entropy alloy WReCrVZr yields a near‑complete single‑phase body‑centered cubic matrix with intermetallic precipitates of the WRe‑rich and V‑rich types. As the overall Re content is increased relative to W, the lattice distortion is enhanced, and solid‑solution strengthening dominates the hardness response; however, beyond a critical Re threshold, the formation of Re‑rich σ‑like intermetallics accelerates, leading to a saturation of hardness because further grain refinement is offset by the coarsening of these secondary phases. When Cr or V concentrations are elevated, the emergence of Cr‑rich Laves‑phase precipitates or V‑rich carbides contributes additional hardening through precipitation strengthening, yet their growth at high sintering temperatures also promotes grain coarsening, partially mitigating the hardness gains. Consequently, the hardness exhibits a peak at intermediate Re/Cr/V ratios where the balance between lattice distortion, solid‑solution strengthening, and fine secondary‑phase dispersion is optimized, and decreases toward compositions dominated by large, sparsely distributed intermetallics.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content

text: In laser‑additive manufactured ZrTiW, the BCC lattice undergoes rapid solidification that generates a highly refined grain structure with pronounced texture along the build direction. This microstructure, combined with substantial lattice distortion from the large size difference among Zr, Ti, and W, enhances solid‑solution strengthening but also predisposes the alloy to intergranular fracture. Three‑point bend fracture toughness tests performed in accordance with ASTM E399/E1820 reveal that the critical stress intensity factor decreases markedly as the notch root radius is reduced from 1 mm to 0.25 mm, indicating pronounced notch sensitivity. The observed reduction is attributed to the accumulation of dislocation pile‑ups at the notch tip and the limited ability of the brittle BCC matrix to redistribute stress through ductile mechanisms. Consequently, fracture toughness is strongly governed by the ease with which a crack initiates from a pre‑existing notch, rather than by bulk material properties alone. This behavior underscores the importance of controlling not only grain size and phase stability but also residual stress gradients and surface finish in laser‑additive processes to mitigate notch‑induced failure in refractory HEAs.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: The TiZrReHf refractory high‑entropy alloy, prepared by successive arc‑melting and rapid drop‑casting, exhibits a pronounced dependence of hardness on the relative amounts of Ti, Zr, Re, and Hf. Increasing the Re content relative to the early‑transition elements promotes the formation of a nanoscale secondary β‑phase with a body‑centered cubic lattice, which is highly coherent with the dominant α‑phase matrix. The coherent interfacial strain and the reduced lattice parameter mismatch lead to enhanced solid‑solution strengthening, reflected in a gradual rise in Vickers hardness as Re rises. Conversely, excessive Ti or Zr, which favor the formation of an intermetallic TiZr₂ type Laves phase, introduce incoherent precipitates that act as weak links; their volume fraction grows with Ti/Zr enrichment, reducing the overall hardness. The optimum hardness is observed at intermediate Re fractions, where the β‑phase is present in fine, uniformly dispersed form without excessive secondary intermetallics, demonstrating the delicate balance between solid‑solution hardening and secondary‑phase brittleness in this system.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content

text: In a powder‑metallurgical study of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrVWReHfMoTi, specimens fabricated by spark plasma sintering exhibited a pronounced decline in both ultimate tensile strength and yield strength with increasing test temperature. At room temperature, the alloy maintained a high yield plateau attributable to the combined solid‑solution hardening of the large atomic‑size mismatch among Zr, V, W, Re, Hf, Mo, and Ti, together with a fine, equiaxed grain population refined through rapid sintering. As temperature rose toward 1000 °C, thermally activated dislocation motion and dynamic recovery reduced the lattice resistance, leading to a marked softening in both strength metrics. Three‑point bend fracture toughness tests, conducted in accordance with ASTM E399/E1820, revealed that the crack‑toughening effect of the persistent dispersion of Re‑rich intermetallics diminished at elevated temperatures due to reduced interfacial coherency strain energy, which in turn amplified crack‑opening stresses and accelerated crack propagation. The correlation between the temperature‑driven loss of lattice distortion strength and the observed reduction in fracture toughness underscores the importance of maintaining fine‑scale, coherent second phases to preserve high‑temperature mechanical performance in this HEA system.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: temperature dependence of tensile strength and yield strength

text: Mechanical alloying of equiatomic NbTaCrMoWReV was carried out in a planetary ball mill for 30 h at 200 rpm using 10:1 ball‑to‑powder ratio; the process produced a homogeneous fine‑grained powder with average particle size below 3 µm. X‑ray diffraction of the milled powder displayed a single bcc phase with broadened peaks indicative of severe lattice distortion arising from the 6.5 at.% atomic‑size mismatch between the constituent elements. Subsequent hot pressing at 1900 °C under 50 MPa for 15 min yielded a near‑fully dense bulk with micro‑porosity below 1 %. Transmission electron microscopy revealed a refined grain structure (≈0.5 µm) and high‑angle annular dark‑field imaging confirmed the random solid‑solution nature of the phase. The pronounced lattice distortion increases the dislocation core energy and reduces the mean free path for dislocation motion, thereby contributing to elevated yield strength and hardness relative to binaries of the same constituent metals.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: lattice distortion effects from atomic size mismatch
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Mechanical alloying of Nb–Cr–Re–Ta–V powders to a uniform 400 nm particle size followed by hot pressing at 1800 °C produced a single‑phase solid solution with a body‑centered cubic lattice. The substantial atomic size mismatch among Nb, Cr, Re, Ta, and V introduces pronounced lattice distortion, which is reflected in the measured yield stress of the sintered alloy. Within this high‑entropy system, the solid‑solution strengthening contribution scales with the mean solute size difference, σ₀·Δr, and the lattice friction parameter, resulting in a pronounced increase in yield strength when the composition is shifted toward elements with larger radii, such as Re. Moreover, the substitutional disorder reduces the mobility of partial dislocations, thereby elevating the critical resolved shear stress. Consequently, the NbCrReTaV alloy displays a markedly higher yield strength compared with equiatomic Nb–Ta–V, confirming that the magnitude of lattice distortion governs the solid‑solution strengthening behavior in this refractory high‑entropy system.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: qualitative yield strength trends and their relation to solid solution strengthening

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy WHfZr, prepared by ball‑mill‑induced powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering, exemplifies how compositional tuning governs elastic stiffness through changes in bonding character. Its bcc lattice contains a high degree of lattice distortion from the large size mismatch among W, Hf, and Zr, which enhances electron density at the interstitial sites and strengthens the covalent‑like d‑band interactions. Consequently, the Young’s modulus rises compared to binary W or HfZr alloys, reflecting the increased resistance to bond stretching. Compression testing of sintered specimens reveals a pronounced yield plateau: as the composition becomes richer in the heavier, more incompressible W, the elastic response dominates and the material remains effectively elastic until a sudden brittle fracture, whereas Hf‑enriched samples display a lower modulus and a more gradual transition to yielding. Thus, the elastic modulus in WHfZr is directly linked to the balance between metallic and covalent bonding contributions, dictating the onset of brittle failure under load.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: elastic (Young's) modulus trends and their relation to bonding character and composition
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy TiZrWCr produced a predominantly body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with only minor secondary phases. X‑ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy reveal that the lattice parameter is intermediate between that of pure Ti, Zr, W, and Cr, indicating extensive lattice distortion due to the four‑element composition and the large size mismatch among the constituents. The homogenized microstructure displays equiaxed grains of 15–20 µm, with no discernible intermetallic precipitates or elemental segregation, confirming the stability of the single‑phase BCC matrix at the melt‑solidification temperature. Thermodynamic assessment based on CALPHAD calculations shows a low Gibbs free‑energy difference between the solid solution and possible competing phases, which rationalizes the observed single‑phase behavior over a wide temperature range. The absence of brittle intermetallics suggests that TiZrWCr retains the desirable combination of high‑temperature strength and toughness associated with BCC refractory HEAs.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: phase stability and the formation of BCC solid solutions

text: Powder‑metallurgy routes were employed to fabricate VWHfTiCrMoTa and TiVHfZrMo, each comprising equiatomic mixtures of the respective refractory elements. After ball‑mill grinding, powders were pre‑compacted and subjected to spark‑plasma sintering at 2000 °C under 50 MPa, yielding dense bulk specimens with porosities below 2 %. Compression tests performed at room temperature revealed a pronounced asymmetry between tensile and compressive yielding: the VWHfTiCrMoTa alloy displayed a higher compressive yield stress compared to its tensile counterpart, a trend attributable to its finer, more homogeneously distributed secondary TiH₂ precipitates that impede dislocation motion preferentially in the compression regime. Conversely, TiVHfZrMo exhibited a comparatively lower compressive yield response, correlating with its coarser Zr‑rich intermetallic clusters that act as weak planes under compressive loading. Grain size refinement during sintering further amplified these effects, with the VWHfTiCrMoTa alloy maintaining a finer microstructure due to the stabilizing influence of Cr, whereas TiVHfZrMo experienced slight grain growth from the Zr‑Zr bonding network. Overall, the microstructural heterogeneities and phase distribution inherent to each composition dictate the observed compressive yield asymmetry.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Powder blends of elemental Mo, Re, Ti, and Ta (nominal equiatomic) were mechanically alloyed for 10 h under argon, producing an average particle size of 50 µm and a narrow size distribution (20–80 µm). The milled powders were uniaxially pressed at 300 MPa into green compacts (25 mm diameter) and then subjected to spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1900 °C under 50 MPa for 5 min, with a heating rate of 100 °C min⁻¹. X‑ray diffraction of the sintered material confirmed a single BCC phase with lattice parameter slightly expanded relative to pure Mo, consistent with lattice distortion from the large atomic radius of Re and the size difference among the constituent elements. Optical microscopy after selective etching revealed pronounced dendritic segregation; Mo‑rich dendrite cores (≈40 µm) were interspersed within a Ti–Ta–Re matrix. SEM back‑scattered imaging showed a coarse grain structure (average size ≈20 µm) with dendrites aligned along the compaction direction, suggesting directional solidification during rapid SPS heating. The dendritic morphology, coupled with the retained elemental segregation, is expected to influence mechanical behavior by providing localized hardening sites and potential pathways for crack initiation.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: microstructural features such as dendritic segregation and grain size

text: The powder‑metallurgy route followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) produces a dense VHfNbTaCrW refractory high‑entropy alloy with a largely body‑centered cubic (BCC) lattice and only minor intermetallic enrichment at the grain boundaries. During SPS, rapid heating and pressure application suppress extensive grain growth, yielding sub‑micron grains that reinforce the solid‑solution matrix. In this multi‑principal system, the large atomic‑size mismatch among V, Hf, Nb, Ta, Cr, and W generates substantial lattice distortion, which enhances dislocation‑solubility interactions and increases the lattice resistance to slip. The fine grain size further augments the yield strength via the Hall–Petch relationship, while the high fraction of substitutional solutes contributes additional solid‑solution strengthening. Together, these mechanisms produce a pronounced rise in yield stress relative to single‑element refractory alloys, and the strength scales with the overall solute concentration, indicating that tailoring the compositional balance can systematically modulate the yield strength without compromising ductility.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: qualitative yield strength trends and their relation to solid solution strengthening

text: Vacuum induction melting of TiHfRe yields a near‑equiatomic bulk ingot that is rapidly solidified to a largely single‑phase body‑centered cubic (bcc) solid solution. Subsequent homogenization at 1700 °C for 24 h under argon reduces compositional gradients that arise from differential segregation during melting. This heat treatment promotes diffusion of Ti, Hf, and Re into the matrix, suppressing the formation of Ti‑rich carbides or intermetallic precipitates that would otherwise nucleate at grain boundaries. As a result, the microstructure evolves to exhibit equiaxed grains with an average size of 10–15 µm and a markedly reduced density of secondary phase particles. The elimination of compositional inhomogeneities enhances lattice distortion uniformly across the alloy, increasing the effective solid solution strengthening contribution. Consequently, the homogenized TiHfRe displays higher yield strength and improved ductility relative to the as‑cast state, while maintaining a low porosity level that is critical for preserving elastic modulus and fracture toughness.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure

text: Mechanical alloying followed by hot‑pressing produces a fine, equiaxed microstructure for both CrWMoVHfTa and ReCrMoTiV, yet their compressive yield responses diverge because of differences in lattice distortion and phase stability. In CrWMoVHfTa, the large atomic size mismatch among Cr, W, Mo, V, Hf, and Ta generates substantial solid‑solution strengthening and a high intrinsic resistance to dislocation glide, which manifests as a pronounced asymmetry: the compressive yield stress exceeds the tensile yield stress by a larger margin. The presence of a minor, coherently dispersed Hf‑rich secondary phase further impedes dislocation motion under compression, amplifying the yield asymmetry. Conversely, ReCrMoTiV exhibits a smaller lattice distortion due to the near‑isoelectronic Re, Cr, Mo, and Ti, and the Ti‑rich matrix promotes the formation of Ti–Re intermetallics that are relatively soft under compression. Consequently, ReCrMoTiV displays a less pronounced compressive‑tensile yield asymmetry and a lower compressive yield stress compared to CrWMoVHfTa, reflecting its weaker solid‑solution strengthening and softer secondary phases.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response

text: Mechanical alloying of the equiatomic refractory HEA TaTiVZrNbHfW was performed in a planetary mill under argon, using 5 wt % milling media for 48 h with 5 min rest intervals; the resulting nanocrystalline powder exhibited a uniform grain size below 50 nm and a pronounced texture owing to preferential orientation of the hexagonal close‑packed sub‑lattice of Zr and Hf. Hot pressing was carried out at 1900 °C under 60 MPa for 5 min in a vacuum furnace, producing fully densified billets with a 3–5 % anisotropy in density due to the directional compaction. Subsequent extrusion at 1500 °C yielded textured rods with a dominant c‑axis alignment along the extrusion direction. Tensile specimens extracted parallel and perpendicular to the extrusion axis displayed markedly different elongation and yield responses: samples oriented along the c‑axis exhibited higher ultimate tensile strength and reduced ductility, attributable to the alignment of dislocation glide planes and the suppression of twinning. Perpendicular specimens, meanwhile, showed enhanced strain‑hardening and greater elongation, reflecting a more isotropic grain boundary network and easier activation of cross‑planar slip systems. These directional disparities confirm that the processing route imposes a strong texture that governs the anisotropy of mechanical behavior in this HEA.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing

text: The vacuum induction melt of VTaTiCrHf produces a body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with a modest lattice distortion (~2 %). The resulting microstructure exhibits a fine equiaxed grain population (average size <10 µm) and a low volume fraction of secondary TiC precipitates, both of which enhance the alloy’s elongation at fracture. The fine grains contribute to a higher strain‑hardening rate, delaying necking, while the coherently dispersed TiC particles act as obstacles to dislocation motion, allowing additional plastic strain before failure. However, the presence of high‑temperature Cr‑rich precipitates along grain boundaries can introduce localized hardening and reduce the overall ductility, particularly under rapid straining conditions. The balance between solid‑solution strengthening from V and Ta and the ductility promoted by fine grains and dispersed second phases ultimately governs the alloy’s fracture elongation, yielding a moderate ductility relative to other refractory HEAs.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: A refractory high entropy alloy comprising W, V, Zr, Mo, and Ta was synthesized by arc melting followed by rapid drop casting into a copper mold. The as‑cast microstructure consists of a predominantly BCC matrix interrupted by fine, irregular intermetallic precipitates enriched in V and Zr, accompanied by compositional fluctuations across the grain boundaries. Subsequent homogenization at 2000 °C for 24 h in an inert atmosphere promoted extensive diffusion of the alloying elements, thereby reducing local compositional gradients and dissolving the V‑rich precipitates into the solid solution. Grain growth proceeded modestly, yielding equiaxed grains of ~10 µm and a more uniform lattice distortion field. Electron backscatter diffraction revealed a significant reduction in low‑angle grain boundaries, while atom probe tomography indicated a homogenized distribution of the five constituents within ±0.5 at %. The refined microstructure, with a decreased secondary phase volume fraction and more uniform solid solution strengthening, is expected to enhance the alloy’s strength and fracture toughness by suppressing micro‑crack initiation sites while maintaining high-temperature stability.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure

text: A vacuum induction melting route was employed to synthesize the refractory high‑entropy alloy ReHfVTaZrMoNb, yielding a bulk ingot that was homogenized by an additional annealing step at 2000 °C. The microstructure exhibited a dual‑phase texture, with a dominant BCC matrix interspersed by fine, lamellar intermetallic precipitates rich in Re and V. Electron backscatter diffraction revealed a mean grain size of ~5 µm, with local refinement to ~1 µm in regions adjacent to the intermetallics. Nanoindentation mapping across these microstructural domains showed that local hardness was markedly higher in the Re–V enriched precipitates, with modulus values exceeding those of the matrix by ~20 %. Correlating these data with tensile testing at room temperature indicated that the alloy’s ultimate tensile strength increased with decreasing average grain size and with a higher volume fraction of the hard intermetallic phase, while the matrix retained sufficient ductility to avoid catastrophic brittle fracture. These trends underscore the role of solid‑solution strengthening from lattice distortion and precipitation hardening in governing the alloy’s macroscopic tensile response.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: qualitative tensile strength trends relative to composition and grain size
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: The work‑hardening response of refractory high‑entropy alloys is governed primarily by lattice distortion, solid‑solution strengthening, and the ease of dislocation nucleation and interaction. In the CrMoZr alloy, the relatively modest size mismatch between Cr, Mo, and Zr generates a moderate lattice distortion that permits dislocations to glide with limited hindrance, resulting in a lower rate of strain hardening after the initial elastic region. Conversely, HfReZrTaWCrMo contains five principal elements with a wide spread in atomic radii; the high lattice distortion enhances short‑range ordering and increases the probability of dislocation‑dislocation and dislocation‑phase interactions. The more complex stacking‑fault energy landscape in the latter alloy leads to a higher density of mobile kinks and a more pronounced back‑stress buildup, producing a steeper hardening curve under tensile loading. Therefore, the HfReZrTaWCrMo alloy is expected to exhibit a higher work‑hardening tendency than CrMoZr, reflected in a steeper increase of flow stress with strain, though both retain the characteristic gradual hardening typical of high‑entropy systems.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: work hardening behavior during tensile deformation
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: In a recent study the refractory high‑entropy alloy TaWNbHfTi was fabricated by suction casting inside an argon‑purged chamber to avoid oxidation. Microstructural examination revealed a predominantly BCC solid solution with a minor intermetallic (Ta, Nb)Ti phase that precipitates along grain boundaries. Hardness measurements across compositional gradients indicate that increasing the fraction of the Ti‑rich intermetallic leads to a pronounced hardening effect, while a more homogenous solid solution tends to soften the material. This trend can be rationalized by the lattice distortion imposed by the large atomic size mismatch between Ta, W, Nb, Hf, and Ti, which enhances solid‑solution strengthening. However, the formation of the Ti‑rich phase introduces hard, coherent precipitates that impede dislocation motion and thereby raise hardness. Consequently, alloys with a higher secondary phase content exhibit superior hardness at the expense of ductility, illustrating the trade‑off between strength and plasticity inherent to this high‑entropy system.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content

text: In comparing the laser‐additive‐manufactured alloys NbVCr and HfTiCrV, hardness trends are governed primarily by the degree of lattice distortion and the propensity to form hard intermetallic or carbides during rapid solidification. The NbVCr system, containing the early transition metal Nb and the smaller V atom, experiences significant size mismatch that promotes solid‐solution strengthening, yet its composition lacks the heavier Hf and Ti that would otherwise enhance interstitial or ternary phase formation. Consequently, NbVCr tends to exhibit moderate hardness, largely derived from fine, homogeneously distributed solid solution strengthening with limited secondary phase content. In contrast, HfTiCrV incorporates the larger Hf and Ti atoms, increasing lattice distortion and fostering the precipitation of hard HfTi‐rich intermetallics and possibly TiC during the rapid cooling of directed energy deposition. These secondary phases are coherent or semi‑coherent with the matrix, providing additional obstruction to dislocation motion and thereby elevating the overall hardness relative to NbVCr. Thus, HfTiCrV would plausibly trend higher in hardness due to its richer secondary phase content and greater lattice distortion.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content

text: In suction‑cast TiNbReZr and CrZrRe alloys processed under a high‑purity argon atmosphere, compressive yield strength exhibits a pronounced asymmetry relative to the tensile response. TiNbReZr, with a body‑centered cubic lattice and a high degree of lattice distortion from the large atomic radii of Ti and Nb relative to Re and Zr, displays a relatively low compressive yield due to the tendency of its dense, high‑temperature β‑phase to undergo localized shear banding under compression; the alloy’s microstructure is further enriched by fine, coherent Zr‑rich precipitates that impede dislocation motion under tension but offer limited resistance to the non‑planar shear systems activated in compression. In contrast, CrZrRe, adopting a more stable face‑centered cubic structure, benefits from the larger Cr‑induced lattice strain and from a higher density of intermetallic Cr‑rich secondary phases that act as effective obstacles to dislocation glide in all crystallographic directions. Consequently, CrZrRe is expected to trend toward a higher compressive yield strength than TiNbReZr, as its microstructural features more uniformly suppress plastic deformation under both tensile and compressive loads.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response

text: Both CrTiMoWTaVHf and HfTaVReW were fabricated by suction casting in a protected argon atmosphere to minimize oxidation. In CrTiMoWTaVHf the high volume fraction of the BCC solid solution phase is interrupted by minor intermetallics such as Cr₂Mo and TiH₂, which act as crack‑tip bridges and promote crack deflection, thereby enhancing fracture toughness. The grain boundary character in this alloy shows a greater proportion of high‑angle boundaries, which impede crack propagation and provide additional energy absorption. Conversely, HfTaVReW contains a more continuous BCC matrix but also a significant fraction of Hf‑rich intermetallic precipitates that form along grain boundaries; these precipitates are more brittle and can act as initiation sites, lowering fracture toughness. The finer average grain size in CrTiMoWTaVHf also contributes to higher toughness by providing more barriers to crack growth. Consequently, CrTiMoWTaVHf would plausibly exhibit a higher fracture toughness than HfTaVReW due to its more favorable phase distribution, boundary character, and crack‑deflection mechanisms.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: fracture toughness trends and their relation to phase content, grain boundary character, and crack path
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: The HfWReNbCr alloy synthesized by high‑energy mechanical alloying and consolidated through hot pressing exhibits pronounced anisotropy in tensile response when fabricated with directional texturing or additive layering. The severe deformation imposed during ball milling creates a high density of subgrains and an elevated lattice distortion that uniformly strengthen all directions, yet the subsequent hot‑pressed microstructure shows preferential alignment of elongated Nb‑rich lamellae and Re‑rich precipitates along the pressing axis. This texture leads to higher yield strength and modulus parallel to the build direction, while the transverse direction displays lower strengths but improved ductility due to the ability of the oriented Cr‑rich columns to absorb shear. The anisotropic hardening originates from directional variations in solid‑solution strengthening and precipitate spacing; lamellae spaced coarsely in the transverse plane permit easier slip, whereas finer spacing along the build axis enhances resistance. Consequently, tensile tests reveal a marked dependence of ultimate tensile strength, strain‑hardening behavior, and fracture toughness on loading orientation, underscoring the need for controlled texture engineering in additive processing of HfWReNbCr.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples

text: Powder‑metallurgy routes followed by spark plasma sintering produced textured VMoZrTiCrReNb and ZrNbMoReTi specimens, enabling a direct assessment of anisotropic tensile behavior. In the VMoZrTiCrReNb alloy, the presence of multiple body‑centered cubic and hexagonal close‑packed constituents yields a pronounced columnar grain texture along the build direction; this promotes higher yield and ultimate tensile stresses when loaded parallel to the texture, but reduced ductility due to limited slip systems on the secondary phases. The ZrNbMoReTi alloy, dominated by a single body‑centered cubic lattice with minimal secondary intermetallics, develops a more isotropic grain distribution; tensile loading along or across the build axis shows comparable strengths, with only modest increases in yield stress parallel to the preferred orientation. Thus, VMoZrTiCrReNb is expected to exhibit stronger anisotropy, displaying higher strength but lower elongation when loaded along the texture direction, whereas ZrNbMoReTi should maintain more uniform tensile properties regardless of loading orientation.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples

text: The MoZrTaVCr alloy, fabricated by suction casting in a high‑purity argon atmosphere, exhibits a dense, columnar γ‑phase matrix with minimal porosity, which strongly influences its high‑temperature oxidation resistance. During exposure to 800 °C in air, a continuous, self‑limiting oxide layer forms predominantly from the rapid oxidation of Zr and Ta, producing ZrO₂ and Ta₂O₅ that adhere closely to the underlying metal. Mo and V, while more soluble in the matrix, tend to remain in the bulk due to their lower affinity for oxygen at this temperature, thereby reducing the overall oxygen uptake. The resulting oxide film displays a graded microstructure: a porous outer region rich in ZrO₂, transitioning to a denser, continuous layer of Ta₂O₅. This architecture suppresses crack initiation and propagation, enhancing oxidation durability. Furthermore, the high lattice distortion inherent to the five‑element system contributes to sluggish diffusion of oxygen through the alloy, slowing the growth rate of the oxide film and preserving mechanical integrity at prolonged service temperatures.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: oxidation behavior at elevated temperature

text: In this comparative study, we investigated the tensile anisotropy of two refractory high‑entropy alloys—NbCrReVTiMo and WTiNbReTaZr—fabricated by laser‑directed energy deposition (DED). The NbCrReVTiMo alloy exhibits a pronounced columnar grain architecture aligned with the build direction, leading to a higher tensile strength and lower ductility along the deposition axis relative to the transverse plane. This anisotropy originates from the strong directional solidification, which promotes solute segregation of Cr and Re, thereby enhancing lattice distortion and solid‑solution strengthening along the build direction. Conversely, the WTiNbReTaZr alloy displays a more equiaxed microstructure with finer, equiaxed Ti–W precipitates uniformly distributed throughout the matrix. The isotropic distribution of these second‑phase particles mitigates directional strengthening, resulting in comparatively lower tensile strength but improved elongation in the build direction. Overall, the NbCrReVTiMo alloy is predicted to show higher tensile strength along the build axis, whereas WTiNbReTaZr offers a more balanced tensile response due to its finer, isotropic microstructural features.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples

text: High‑temperature tensile testing of the refractory high‑entropy alloy HfMoWTaReZr fabricated by powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering reveals a pronounced increase in yield strength relative to binary baselines, attributable to substantial lattice distortion inherent to the multi‑component solid solution. In the 800–1200 °C testing window, the alloy consistently exhibits higher yield stresses than any constituent pair, supporting the hypothesis that the combined atomic radius mismatch and electronegativity differences of Hf, Mo, W, Ta, Re, and Zr amplify the lattice strain field and impede dislocation motion. Grain refinement induced by rapid sintering kinetics further contributes to strengthening, as the smaller, equiaxed grains present a greater density of high‑angle boundaries that act as effective dislocation barriers. The measured yield strength displays a mild temperature dependence, decreasing modestly with increasing test temperature, yet remaining superior to conventional refractory alloys, underscoring the dominant role of solid solution strengthening in governing the mechanical performance of this complex system.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: qualitative yield strength trends and their relation to solid solution strengthening

text: The WTiHfCr high‑entropy alloy, fabricated by ball‑milled powders followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS), exhibits a complex microstructure composed of a BCC solid solution interspersed with nanoscale Ti‑rich precipitates and trace intermetallics. When subjected to Rockwell hardness testing at increasing load increments, the measured hardness values rise more steeply at higher indentation forces, revealing pronounced strain‑rate sensitivity of the material’s strength. This trend can be traced to the limited mobility of dislocations within the heavily distorted lattice, where the large atomic size mismatch between W, Ti, Hf, and Cr promotes short‑range order and constrains slip. At higher indentation rates, the dislocation density surges, forcing more frequent interaction with the Ti‑rich precipitates, which act as obstacles to glide. Consequently, the alloy’s resistance to plastic deformation increases with indentation speed, as reflected in the enhanced Rockwell hardness values.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: strain rate sensitivity of strength properties

text: The powder‑metallurgy route followed by spark‑plasma sintering produced fine, equiaxed grains in both HfNbZrMoReCrW and NbVTi, yet the average grain diameter of the former is consistently larger, typically in the 2–3 µm range, whereas NbVTi averages near 1 µm. In a Hall‑Petch framework, the finer NbVTi microstructure should generate a higher dislocation‑pile‑up resistance, yielding both greater hardness and yield strength compared with HfNbZrMoReCrW. This trend is further amplified by the lower lattice distortion in NbVTi, which allows a more uniform stress field across grain boundaries. Conversely, the relatively coarse grains in HfNbZrMoReCrW reduce the barrier effect of grain boundaries, leading to a softer response under load. Thus, the mechanical performance hierarchy aligns with grain size: NbVTi is expected to exhibit higher hardness and strength, while HfNbZrMoReCrW may show comparatively lower values, reflecting its larger grain population.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: the relationship between grain size and both strength and hardness (Hall-Petch-type reasoning)

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ReMoWVNbCrTa followed by water‑quench forging produced a near‑equiatomic microstructure dominated by a single body‑centered cubic phase with trace TiC‑like secondary precipitates. Standard tensile tests performed under ASTM E8 reveal a pronounced ductility‑strength trade‑off: incremental increases in yield strength and ultimate tensile strength are attained at higher alloying levels of Re and W, which introduce substantial lattice distortion and solid‑solution hardening. However, these same additions promote localized shear banding and early crack initiation, resulting in a marked reduction in uniform and total elongation. The observed softening of the alloy at elevated strain rates correlates with the coarsening of the secondary Cr‑rich precipitates, which disrupt the continuity of the BCC matrix and lower the strain‑hardening capacity. Thus, while the alloy achieves superior strength through enhanced lattice distortion and solid‑solution effects, its elongation is compromised by the concomitant reduction in strain‑hardening ability and the propensity for shear‑band‑driven fracture.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: ductility-strength trade-offs (how gains in strength typically come at the cost of elongation)

text: A refractory high entropy alloy composed of TaNbVReMoZr was synthesized by suction casting within an argon‑purged chamber to suppress oxidation and ensure a uniform microstructure. The resulting alloy exhibited a dense, single‑phase bcc matrix with nanometer‑scale coherent precipitates of (Mo,Re) rich sub‑lamellae. Cyclic tensile–tensile testing revealed a fatigue life that decreases sharply with increasing mean stress, yet remains substantially higher than conventional bcc alloys of similar composition. Detailed crack initiation studies indicated that micro‑cracks preferentially form at sites of localized lattice distortion, where the large atomic size mismatch between Ta and V induces dislocation pile‑ups. Subsequent crack propagation proceeds through a mixed mode of intergranular and transgranular fracture; the fine secondary precipitates impede crack advance by acting as obstacle pinning points, effectively increasing the crack‑tip shielding. Consequently, the alloy’s fatigue endurance is governed by the synergy between solid solution strengthening, the high density of coherent nanoscale precipitates, and the suppression of porosity during rapid solidification, underscoring the critical role of processing‑controlled microstructure in tailoring fatigue performance.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy NbVWMoRe under an inert argon atmosphere produced dense, columnar‑grained microstructures with minor oxide inclusions. Vickers microhardness measurements performed at 4.9 N loading over twenty sites revealed a consistent hardness band of 2600–2800 HV, with local peaks approaching 2900 HV in regions adjacent to coarse intergranular Mo‑rich precipitates. The uniform hardness distribution implies effective solid‑solution strengthening from the large lattice distortion inherent to the Nb/V/W/Mo/Re system, while the modest hardness variation indicates limited secondary‑phase contribution. Notch‑sensitive fracture tests on miniature V‑shaped specimens showed a pronounced drop in fracture toughness relative to polished samples, suggesting that the high hardness, low fracture strain, and the predominance of BCC bonding render the alloy particularly susceptible to crack initiation at geometric stress concentrators. The correlation between localized hardness elevations and reduced energy absorption before catastrophic failure underscores the importance of minimizing micro‑defects and optimizing grain size to mitigate notch sensitivity in this brittle HEA.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: In laser‑additive‑manufactured specimens of the refractory high‑entropy alloys TaZrReWCrHf and NbHfTaTi, the evolution of work‑hardening during tensile testing reflects differences in lattice distortion, slip system activation, and secondary phase stability. The TaZrReWCrHf alloy possesses a higher average atomic radius mismatch, which intensifies lattice distortion and enhances solid‑solution hardening; this leads to a pronounced initial hardening rate as dislocations encounter a highly irregular potential energy landscape. Furthermore, the coexistence of minor intermetallic precipitates (e.g., Cr‑rich phases) pin moving dislocations and sustain strain‑hardening over a broader deformation range. In contrast, NbHfTaTi exhibits a more coherent solid solution with smaller lattice distortion and a reduced population of secondary phases, which allows dislocations to glide more readily and results in a more modest hardening slope. Consequently, TaZrReWCrHf is expected to display a higher work‑hardening trend throughout tensile deformation, while NbHfTaTi will exhibit a relatively lower hardening rate.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: work hardening behavior during tensile deformation

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy VWZrMoHfNb was carried out in a water‑cooled, 12 kA, 50 kHz induction coil, ensuring a molten pool temperature above 2500 °C and a short solidification time that promotes a fine, equiaxed primary β‑phase with minor dendritic Mo–Zr rich lamellae. After cast ingots were solution‑annealed at 1750 °C for 30 h to homogenize the elemental distribution, specimens were polished to a 1 µm finish and then subjected to a high‑temperature plasma spray coating of Al₂O₃/SiC composite. The resulting ceramic layer, ~80 µm thick, adheres through interdiffusion of SiC and the underlying Ti‑rich surface, forming a continuous Si–C–O interlayer that mitigates oxidation at 1200 °C. In situ high‑temperature tribometry revealed that the ceramic barrier reduces surface grain growth and suppresses the nucleation of detrimental ZrO₂ phases, thereby preserving the alloy’s high‑temperature strength and resisting creep deformation.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting

text: In the refractory high‑entropy alloy MoTiHfWTaCrNb produced by mechanical alloying and subsequent hot pressing, the refined microstructure is dominated by a body‑centered cubic matrix with a fine, equiaxed grain size that typically falls below 2 µm. Mechanical alloying introduces severe plastic deformation and high defect densities, which, after consolidation, act as effective grain‑refining agents. According to Hall–Petch considerations, the yield strength and hardness of this alloy increase markedly as the grain boundary area per unit volume grows; the dense network of low‑angle grain boundaries impedes dislocation motion by presenting a higher density of obstacle barriers. Consequently, samples with a smaller average grain size exhibit higher hardness and yield strength, while coarsening during post‑processing or prolonged annealing reduces these attributes. This relationship underscores the importance of controlling the milling duration and compaction parameters to tailor the grain size and thus the mechanical performance of MoTiHfWTaCrNb.

text: Powders of Nb₁₀₀₋ₓWₓHf and Cr₁₀₀₋ₓWₓTa were prepared by high‑energy ball milling under argon, sieved to <45 µm, and compacted into green compacts at 600 MPa before spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 2000 °C for 5 min with a heating rate of 200 °C min⁻¹. The resulting microstructures were characterized by SEM and EBSD; NbWHf exhibited a predominantly body‑centered cubic lattice with a narrow grain size distribution (~5 µm) and minor second‑phase Hf–W carbides, whereas CrWTa showed a more heterogeneous grain size (~10 µm) and pronounced lamellar Cr–W precipitates. Compression tests performed at 500 °C revealed a markedly lower compressive yield stress for CrWTa compared to NbWHf, reflecting the larger grain size and the strengthening‑relief effect of the Cr‑rich precipitates that impede dislocation motion under compressive loading. In contrast, tensile tests on the same specimens displayed a smaller asymmetry, suggesting that the body‑centered cubic matrix of NbWHf maintains more isotropic slip systems, whereas the lamellar precipitates in CrWTa create a more pronounced anisotropic response, thereby lowering its compressive yield relative to its tensile counterpart.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response

text: Samples of the refractory high‑entropy alloy Nb₁₀W₁₀V₁₀Cr₁₀Ta₁₀Mo₁₀Zr₁₀ (wt%) were synthesized by vacuum induction melting with an initial composition matched to the equiatomic target. Melted ingots were remelted at least three times to ensure homogeneity, then hot‑isostatically pressed to 90 % theoretical density before being water‑quenched to retain the single‑phase BCC solid solution. Microstructural examination revealed a fine, nearly equiaxed grain size of 5–10 µm, with occasional nanometric precipitates of a secondary V-rich phase. Compression tests performed at room temperature displayed a yield stress significantly higher than the corresponding tensile yield stress, suggesting a pronounced asymmetry. This disparity correlates with the high lattice distortion imposed by the wide range of atomic radii, which promotes a stronger resistance to dislocation glide under compressive loading due to the increased population of compression‑active slip systems. In contrast, tensile loading activates slip systems more easily, resulting in a lower yield point. The asymmetry is further accentuated by the presence of the V-rich precipitates, which act as effective barriers to dislocation motion predominantly under compression.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response
