text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy WTaMo, synthesized by suction casting under an argon atmosphere, exhibits a pronounced dependence of its strength on deformation rate, a phenomenon that is readily observed in three‑point bend fracture toughness tests conducted per ASTM E399/E1820. During rapid loading, the alloy’s fine equiaxed grains—typically 20–30 µm due to the rapid solidification of the cast—confer a higher yield strength because dislocation motion is impeded by grain boundary obstacles. As the strain rate increases, the limited time for dislocation climb and glide leads to an enhanced work‑hardening rate, shifting the stress–strain curve toward higher stresses and reducing the fracture toughness increment. Conversely, at lower strain rates the alloy’s lattice distortion, arising from the large atomic size mismatch among W, Ta, and Mo, allows for more time for dislocation nucleation and recovery, thereby lowering the effective strength and increasing ductility. Thus, the measured fracture toughness shows a clear decline with increasing strain rate, reflecting the underlying rate‑dependent solid‑solution strengthening and limited grain boundary sliding in the WTaMo matrix.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: strain rate sensitivity of strength properties
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: The microstructural analysis of the two refractory high entropy alloys processed by mechanical alloying and hot‑pressing reveals a clear link between secondary phase formation and hardness. TaReCrHfNb, with its near‑equimolar mixture of transition metals and a comparatively lower Re content, tends to develop a finer dispersion of intermetallic precipitates such as TaNb and CrHf. These nanoscale coherent second phases, coupled with substantial lattice distortion from the size mismatch among Ta, Re, Cr, Hf, and Nb, generate pronounced solid‑solution strengthening and a higher overall hardness. In contrast, ReVTaZrCrHfW contains a higher proportion of V and W, which promote the nucleation of more extensive, coarser secondary phases like ReV and ZrW intermetallics that are less coherent with the matrix. The larger precipitate spacing in this alloy reduces the effectiveness of precipitate strengthening, leading to a comparatively lower hardness. Consequently, TaReCrHfNb is expected to exhibit higher hardness than ReVTaZrCrHfW due to its finer, more coherent secondary phase distribution and greater lattice distortion.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content

text: Suction casting of the equiatomic TiReZrMoWNb alloy was carried out under a purified argon atmosphere to suppress oxidation; a high‑frequency ultrasonic probe was employed to promote rapid solidification and minimize porosity. The resulting cast ingots were homogenized at 1900 °C for 12 h and subsequently water‑quenched to retain a fine, BCC‑dominated microstructure with a primary phase comprising a near‑solid solution of all constituents. Notched tensile specimens (V‑notches, 0.25 mm tip radius) were prepared using a diamond saw, and notch sensitivity was evaluated by measuring the ratio of notched to unnotched yield stresses. Fracture surfaces exhibited intergranular brittle cleavage with minimal plastic dimpling, indicating that the high lattice distortion and limited solute segregation impede dislocation motion. Consequently, the alloy displays elevated notch sensitivity, which correlates with a reduced fracture toughness relative to its unnotched counterpart; the brittle BCC matrix facilitates rapid crack propagation once a critical stress intensity is attained.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Laser additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ReHfV by directed energy deposition produces a predominantly BCC solid solution despite the strong atomic size mismatch among Re, Hf, and V. Rapid solidification during deposition limits the diffusion of elements, suppressing the segregation that would otherwise drive the formation of Hf‑rich or Re‑rich intermetallic phases. Consequently, the microstructure consists of a fine‑grained BCC matrix with only trace amounts of secondary phases, ensuring uniform lattice distortion and strong solid‑solution strengthening. The high processing temperature and short cooling times maintain the equilibrium BCC phase field, preventing the thermodynamically favored HCP or Laves phase transformations that occur in slower cast counterparts. Uniform elemental distribution within the BCC lattice promotes phase stability, as evidenced by the absence of detectable phase boundaries in diffraction studies. Overall, laser additive manufacturing preserves the desired single‑phase BCC structure in ReHfV, which is critical for achieving consistent mechanical performance.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: phase stability and the formation of BCC solid solutions

text: High‑entropy alloy HfReMoZrTa was synthesized by ball‑mill mechanical alloying and consolidated via hot pressing at 1900 °C under argon, yielding a dense, single‑phase BCC microstructure with a mean grain size of ~10 µm and minimal porosity. In situ tensile tests conducted up to 1700 °C in a controlled‑atmosphere furnace revealed pronounced notch sensitivity, with pre‑cracked specimens exhibiting a substantial drop in apparent fracture toughness relative to unnotched counterparts. Analysis of fracture surfaces showed intergranular cracking initiated at grain boundaries proximal to the notch tip, suggesting that lattice distortion induced by the high configurational entropy enhances local stress concentration and promotes brittle cleavage. The lack of secondary phases or fine precipitates means that solid‑solution strengthening dominates, but it does not mitigate the intrinsic brittleness of the BCC lattice at elevated temperatures. Consequently, the alloy displays a marked decrease in toughness with increasing notch size, underscoring the critical role of grain‑boundary engineering in controlling notch‑sensitive fracture behavior in refractory high‑entropy systems.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: Both refractory high‑entropy alloys, HfTiTaCrZrW and ZrTiReCrNbW, were fabricated by arc melting and subsequent drop casting, yielding largely single‑phase BCC structures with minor secondary intermetallics. In HfTiTaCrZrW, the relatively uniform grain boundary character, dominated by high‑angle boundaries with low excess energy, facilitates crack blunting and promotes ductile fracture mechanisms, leading to a comparatively higher fracture toughness. Conversely, ZrTiReCrNbW contains a higher fraction of low‑angle boundaries and a modest precipitation of Cr‑rich Laves‑type intermetallics at the grain periphery; these features act as preferential crack initiation sites and constrain crack deflection, reducing toughness. The contrast in phase content—minimal secondary phases in HfTiTaCrZrW versus pronounced intermetallic precipitation in ZrTiReCrNbW—combined with the differences in grain boundary chemistry, thus drives the observed fracture toughness trend, with HfTiTaCrZrW expected to outperform ZrTiReCrNbW.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: fracture toughness trends and their relation to phase content, grain boundary character, and crack path

text: Mechanical alloying of the NbTiMoTaW alloy was conducted in a high‑energy planetary mill under argon, using a 10:1 powder to milling media ratio and 600 rpm for 30 h with intermittent 30‑min rest intervals. The resulting nanocrystalline powder exhibited an average crystallite size of ~50 nm, with a pronounced solid solution of Nb, Ti, Mo, Ta, and W on a body‑centered cubic lattice. Subsequent hot pressing at 1850 °C in a vacuum furnace for 2 h produced dense compacts (density > 99 % theoretical) with columnar grains elongated along the pressing axis, average width ~2 µm. X‑ray diffraction revealed only the primary bcc phase, but high‑resolution TEM showed fine Ti‑rich secondary precipitates (≤ 20 nm) dispersed throughout the matrix. In high‑temperature mechanical tests, the NbTiMoTaW alloy maintained superior creep resistance above 1400 °C relative to conventional Ni‑based superalloys, attributable to the stronger lattice distortion and higher melting point constituents. Its fracture toughness at 1200 °C remained comparable, while its yield strength displayed a modest decline with increasing temperature, consistent with the predicted thermal softening of bcc high‑entropy systems.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: comparison with conventional Ni-based superalloys in high-temperature contexts
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Mechanical alloying of V, Zr, Mo, and Ta powders followed by hot pressing produced a VZrMoTa refractory high entropy alloy exhibiting a fully equiaxed microstructure with average grain size near 2 µm. The solid solution strengthening mechanism inherent to the high lattice distortion of the bcc matrix dominates the tensile response, and systematic compositional variations reveal that increasing the V content relative to Zr and Ta sharpens the peak stress at room temperature, while Mo enrichment enhances the high‑temperature strength through the development of fine, coherent Zr‑rich lamellae that act as effective obstacle plates to dislocation glide. Grain size refinement through extended milling further elevates the yield and ultimate tensile stresses, consistent with the Hall–Petch relationship, whereas coarsening during hot pressing diminishes the strength and promotes localized necking. Overall, the alloy shows a strong dependence of tensile strength on the relative proportions of V, Zr, Mo, and Ta, with the combination of high lattice distortion and fine grains providing a synergistic pathway to superior strength in this system.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: qualitative tensile strength trends relative to composition and grain size

text: Powders of Nb, Ti, and Ta were mixed by ball‑milling under argon, then consolidated by spark plasma sintering at 1700 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa. The resulting compacts exhibited a homogeneous body‑centered cubic (bcc) lattice with a modest amount of secondary Ti‑rich intermetallics. Optical and electron‑probe analyses revealed that the average grain diameter ranged from 5 µm to 30 µm, depending on the sintering dwell time and cooling rate. As grain size decreased, the alloy’s microhardness progressively increased, consistent with a Hall‑Petch relationship where the yield strength rises linearly with inverse grain dimension. Transmission electron microscopy showed that finer grains provided a greater density of grain boundary planes, effectively impeding dislocation motion and thereby enhancing both the yield stress and the Vickers hardness. Conversely, coarser grains exhibited reduced hardness and a lower apparent flow stress, illustrating the critical role of grain refinement in optimizing the mechanical performance of NbTiTa.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: the relationship between grain size and both strength and hardness (Hall-Petch-type reasoning)
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: High‑temperature surface protection of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ReTaNbHfTiWZr was examined after synthesis by arc melting and subsequent drop casting, which promotes rapid solidification and a fine, equiaxed microstructure. The alloy exhibits a nearly single‑phase bcc matrix with minor intermetallic precipitates (Re‑rich and Ta–W intermetallics) that provide lattice distortion and solid‑solution strengthening at elevated temperatures. Surface oxidation resistance was enhanced by applying a plasma‑sprayed TiN/Al₂O₃ composite coating that adheres through interdiffusion of Ti and Al into the alloy, forming a continuous barrier of TiO₂ and Al₂O₃. The coating thickness, controlled between 50–80 µm, suppresses the formation of Re‑rich oxides and reduces the rate of grain growth during high‑temperature exposure, thereby preserving the fine grain size that underpins high hardness and yield strength. Thermally induced interdiffusion at the coating‑substrate interface generates a graded transition layer that mitigates thermal mismatch stresses, preventing crack initiation during cyclic oxidation. Overall, the combined microstructural refinement and engineered barrier layers promote sustained mechanical performance and resistance to oxidation for high‑temperature coating applications.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: high-temperature coating or surface protection strategies

text: In the refractory high‑entropy alloy MoHfZrWTi fabricated by laser‑directed energy deposition, the balance between strength and ductility is governed by the interplay of lattice distortion and microstructural refinement. The large atomic size differences among Mo, Hf, Zr, W, and Ti impose severe solid‑solution strain fields that impede dislocation glide, yielding a high intrinsic strength. Simultaneously, rapid solidification in additive manufacturing produces a highly refined columnar‑grain texture with sub‑micron intergranular spacing, further elevating strength through grain‑size‑dependent mechanisms. However, these same features restrict the material’s ability to undergo uniform plastic flow; the dense forest of solute‑induced obstacles elevates the critical resolved shear stress, causing localized shear band initiation. Consequently, the alloy exhibits high yield and ultimate strengths but reduced elongation at fracture, reflecting the classic ductility‑strength trade‑off intrinsic to highly distorted, fine‑grained refractory HEAs.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: ductility-strength trade-offs (how gains in strength typically come at the cost of elongation)
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: The two refractory high‑entropy alloys, HfCrTaZrVMoRe and VTaCr, produced by mechanical alloying and subsequent hot pressing, exhibit markedly different microstructural defect populations that influence their fracture toughness and fatigue life. In the six‑element alloy, the high lattice distortion and complex chemical short‑range order encourage the formation of a fine, homogenous solid solution, but the large number of constituent elements also promotes the persistence of residual porosity and micro‑cracks if the compaction pressure is insufficient. These porosity sites act as stress concentrators, initiating crack propagation under cyclic loading and reducing both the critical stress intensity factor and the endurance limit. The three‑element alloy, with a simpler composition, achieves a denser microstructure during hot pressing, yielding fewer voids and a more continuous grain boundary network. Consequently, VTaCr typically shows improved resistance to crack initiation and slower fatigue crack growth, translating into higher fracture toughness and fatigue performance relative to HfCrTaZrVMoRe, especially when processing conditions are carefully optimized to minimize defects.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: the effect of porosity or processing defects on fracture toughness and fatigue performance
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Both VZrHfReTaCrW and WMoReNbTaHf were fabricated by identical powder metallurgy routes followed by spark plasma sintering, ensuring comparable densification and residual porosity. In VZrHfReTaCrW the high fraction of Zr and Hf, both with large atomic radii, imposes significant lattice distortion, enhancing solid‑solution strengthening relative to WMoReNbTaHf, which contains more transition metals with smaller size mismatches. The presence of V and Cr in the first alloy also promotes a more complex solid solution, further impeding dislocation motion. Grain size evolution during sintering is largely controlled by the sintering temperature and dwell time; the VZrHfReTaCrW matrix tends to retain a finer microstructure because the Zr/Hf network acts as a barrier to grain growth, whereas the W‑rich matrix in WMoReNbTaHf exhibits slightly coarser grains. Consequently, the VZrHfReTaCrW alloy is expected to display a higher tensile strength at room temperature, while the WMoReNbTaHf alloy may achieve a modestly lower strength but potentially better ductility due to its finer lattice distortion and more uniform grain boundary cohesion.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: qualitative tensile strength trends relative to composition and grain size
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing produced dense bulk samples of the refractory high‑entropy alloys TaReNbZrW and MoTiWVCrReHf, allowing direct comparison of how processing‑induced porosity and microstructural defects influence fracture toughness and fatigue life. In the TaReNbZrW alloy, the high‑temperature annealing step after hot pressing reduced residual porosity to below 1 % by volume and promoted the formation of a fine, homogeneous γ‑phase with minimal interfacial segregation. This homogeneous microstructure and low defect density translate into a relatively high resistance to crack initiation and a more gradual fracture energy absorption, yielding superior fracture toughness and extended low‑cycle fatigue life. Conversely, the MoTiWVCrReHf alloy retained a higher residual porosity content due to its higher sintering temperature and more pronounced grain boundary segregation. These porosity sites act as preferential crack nucleation sites, reducing the energy required for crack propagation and leading to a comparatively lower fracture toughness and reduced fatigue endurance. The contrasting behaviors underscore the critical role of processing defects in dictating the mechanical resilience of refractory high‑entropy alloys.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: the effect of porosity or processing defects on fracture toughness and fatigue performance

text: Suction casting of the refractory high entropy alloy ZrCrW under a continuous argon atmosphere yielded fully dense ingots with a single BCC solid solution matrix interspersed by finely distributed secondary Zr-rich precipitates. Instrumented nanoindentation performed on polished cross‑sections revealed a pronounced elevation of hardness in regions containing a higher volume fraction of these coherent precipitates, with a corresponding slight increase in the measured elastic modulus. Quantitative analysis of load–displacement curves showed that the hardness increment correlates linearly with the precipitate volume fraction up to a critical threshold beyond which the hardening plateaued, suggesting a transition from a strength‑increasing regime to one dominated by precipitate–matrix interactions that limit further strengthening. Microstructural characterization by transmission electron microscopy confirmed that the precipitates are coherent with the BCC matrix, maintaining low interfacial energies and thus contributing to the observed mechanical enhancement. These results underscore the pivotal role of secondary phase engineering in tailoring the hardness of ZrCrW high entropy alloys.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: the effect of secondary phase or precipitate content on hardness

text: The NbTaCrTiHfReV alloy, synthesized by high‑energy ball milling followed by uniaxial hot‑pressing, exhibits pronounced lattice distortion owing to the wide spread of atomic radii among its constituent elements. The size difference between large Hf (1.75 Å) and small V (1.34 Å) atoms introduces a substantial local strain field, while the intermediate sizes of Nb, Ta, Cr, Ti, and Re contribute to an overall root‑mean‑square mismatch exceeding 5 %. This distortion disrupts the periodic lattice, elevating the critical resolved shear stress for dislocation glide and thereby enhancing solid‑solution strengthening. During compaction, the high strain energy is partly relieved by the formation of nanoscale, coherently precipitated Ti–V rich intermetallics, which further impede dislocation motion through Orowan looping. Consequently, the alloy displays a higher yield strength and hardness relative to its binary counterparts, while the residual micro‑strain promotes a more ductile fracture behavior by facilitating energy dissipation during plastic deformation.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: lattice distortion effects from atomic size mismatch

text: The vacuum‑induction‑melted refractory high‑entropy alloy CrZrVReWTi exhibits a body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution that is markedly more resistant to grain coarsening than the face‑centered cubic (FCC) matrix of conventional Ni‑based superalloys. The large atomic size mismatch among Cr, Zr, V, Re, W, and Ti produces severe lattice distortion, which impedes dislocation glide and enhances high‑temperature yield strength without the need for γ′ precipitates. In contrast, Ni superalloys rely on coherent intermetallic islands for strength, and their performance deteriorates once these precipitates dissolve or coarsen above ~1100 °C. The CrZrVReWTi alloy maintains a fine, stable grain boundary network and lacks the brittle intermetallics that can embrittle Ni alloys at extreme temperatures, thereby preserving ductility. Furthermore, the absence of carbides in the alloy reduces the propensity for thermal creep damage, while the intrinsic high melting points of Re and W contribute to superior oxidation resistance. Consequently, CrZrVReWTi demonstrates a more consistent mechanical response across the 800–1200 °C range, offering an attractive high‑temperature alternative to Ni‑based superalloys for advanced turbine or high‑speed engine applications.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: comparison with conventional Ni-based superalloys in high-temperature contexts

text: Powder blends of Ta, V, Zr, W, and Hf were prepared by high‑energy ball milling under Ar to achieve <20 µm average particle size and a narrow size distribution. The milled powders were uniaxially compacted at 400 MPa and then sintered in a spark‑plasma device at 2100 °C for 120 s under 50 MPa pressure to obtain fully dense samples (≈99 % theoretical density). Compression tests were carried out on cylindrical specimens (Ø 5 mm × 10 mm) with notched and unnotched geometries; notch radii ranged from 0.5 to 1.0 mm. The notched samples displayed a pronounced drop in apparent yield stress compared to their unnotched counterparts, indicating a high notch sensitivity characteristic of brittle BCC matrices. Post‑fracture examination revealed that the fracture surfaces exhibited a predominantly transgranular, cleavage‑like morphology, and the crack initiation sites were closely associated with localized lattice distortion at grain boundaries. These observations suggest that the limited plastic accommodation of the TaVZrWHf microstructure amplifies stress concentrations at notches, thereby reducing fracture toughness in this high‑entropy system.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: The VReTiMoTa alloy synthesized by powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering exhibited a microstructure dominated by a single bcc solid solution with minor Ti-rich intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries. Crack propagation experiments revealed that fracture toughness was highest when the intermetallic volume fraction was kept below 5 vol.% and the grain boundary character remained largely high-angle, which promoted grain boundary decohesion rather than crack advance along the lattice. When the Ti-rich phase grew beyond this threshold, its brittleness induced local stress concentration, causing cracks to deflect along the weak intermetallic interfaces and leading to a sharp drop in toughness. Moreover, fine equiaxed grains (<10 µm) constrained the initiation of transgranular cracks, whereas coarsened grains favored ductile transgranular fracture. Thus, maintaining a low secondary phase content and a high proportion of high-angle grain boundaries, coupled with refined grain size, was critical to preserving the intrinsic fracture resistance of this refractory HEA.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: fracture toughness trends and their relation to phase content, grain boundary character, and crack path

text: Vacuum induction melting of NbHfMoZr produces a single‑phase bcc solid solution with minor oxide inclusions. X‑ray diffraction shows lattice parameter expansion relative to pure Nb, indicating significant lattice distortion from the large Hf and Zr atoms. Elastic modulus measurements on polished specimens reveal a monotonic increase with Hf content, consistent with the higher valence electron concentration and stronger metallic bonding expected for Hf. The measured Young’s modulus approaches the theoretical value predicted by the rule‑of‑mixtures for the constituent elements, underscoring the dominance of covalent‑metallic hybridization in this system. Grain size refinement achieved by rapid quenching reduces the compliance of the alloy, further elevating modulus values, while secondary ZrO₂ particles provide constrained interfaces that restrict lattice strain. These observations collectively suggest that tailoring the Hf/Zr ratio and processing parameters to maximize lattice distortion and minimize porosity can systematically elevate the elastic modulus of NbHfMoZr alloys, offering a pathway toward high‑performance refractory structural components.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: elastic (Young's) modulus trends and their relation to bonding character and composition

text: Mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing was employed to synthesize the refractory high‑entropy alloy HfCrTiZrMoWNb. X‑ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy revealed that the primary BCC solid solution is accompanied by fine secondary precipitates of TiZrO and a minor Nb‑rich intermetallic phase. The precipitate distribution is strongly dependent on the milling duration and the subsequent densification temperature; extended milling promotes finer, more uniformly dispersed precipitates, whereas higher pressing temperatures lead to coarsening and occasional agglomeration. Hardness measurements indicate that the volume fraction and size of these secondary phases exert a pronounced influence: higher precipitate volume fractions correlate with increased hardness due to impeded dislocation motion, while coarsened precipitates diminish the hardening effect by reducing the effective barrier density. Consequently, tailoring the mechanical alloying parameters to control precipitate size and distribution offers a viable strategy to modulate the hardness of HfCrTiZrMoWNb without significantly affecting its bulk density or overall microstructure.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: the effect of secondary phase or precipitate content on hardness

text: Arc‐melting and subsequent drop casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy WTaZrCrNbTiHf produce a largely single‑phase bcc matrix with modest dendritic segregation of the more noble elements. At temperatures above 900 °C, the alloy exhibits a self‑limited oxidation layer dominated by stable metal oxides of Ta and W that nucleate on the surface and grow outward in a columnar fashion, restricting further oxygen penetration. The presence of Zr and Hf enhances the formation of a continuous, adherent ZrO₂/HfO₂ interfacial film, which acts as a barrier to diffusion and mitigates microcracking that typically accompanies rapid oxide growth. Minor Ti and Nb oxides, while less stable, contribute to the overall oxide thickness through secondary reaction pathways that release trapped oxygen, thus preserving the integrity of the protective layer. The overall oxidation resistance is therefore governed by the synergistic formation of a composite oxide skin that balances high‑temperature stability with low diffusivity, resulting in a markedly reduced mass gain compared to binary refractory counterparts.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: oxidation behavior at elevated temperature

text: The powder‑metallurgy route followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) produced dense bulk specimens of WTaVCr and HfReVTiCr, yet the two refractory high‑entropy alloys exhibit distinct ductility behaviors. In WTaVCr the dominant solid‑solution strengthening arises from the large lattice distortion imposed by the heavy W and V atoms, which narrows the grain size to sub‑micron scale through rapid SPS densification. The fine, equiaxed grains impede dislocation motion but also favor homogeneous stress distribution, allowing a moderate elongation at fracture. Conversely, HfReVTiCr contains a significant fraction of Hf, which promotes the precipitation of Ti‑rich secondary phases during SPS cooling. These coherent precipitates refine the microstructure but introduce localized stress concentrations that facilitate crack initiation, thereby reducing elongation relative to WTaVCr. Thus, while both alloys maintain high strength, the grain‑size‑controlled WTaVCr is expected to display a higher ductility trend than HfReVTiCr due to its more uniform microstructure and fewer brittle secondary phases.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: The comparative study of the two BCC refractory high‑entropy alloys, WNbHfZrReV and VTiRe, both fabricated by powder metallurgy followed by spark‑plasma sintering, indicates a distinct divergence in notch sensitivity that directly informs fracture‑toughness behavior. In WNbHfZrReV, the high atomic‑number constituents (W, Nb, Hf) generate substantial lattice distortion, which promotes a finer, more uniformly distributed grain structure during sintering. This fine‑grained microstructure, combined with minimal secondary‑phase segregation, limits crack‑tip stress concentrations, thereby reducing notch sensitivity and enabling a comparatively higher fracture toughness. Conversely, VTiRe contains a lower‑Z element (V) and a higher proportion of Ti, which tends to form coarse, intergranular Ti-rich precipitates during sintering. These precipitates act as sites for stress‑concentration and facilitate intergranular cracking initiated at notches, thereby increasing notch sensitivity and lowering overall fracture toughness. Hence, WNbHfZrReV is likely to exhibit a higher fracture‑toughness response, whereas VTiRe would trend toward greater brittleness under notched conditions.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: Laser additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloys ZrHfReTi and VZrCr was performed by directed energy deposition under identical process parameters to enable a direct comparison of microstructural evolution and hardness. The ZrHfReTi composition exhibited a more homogeneous solid‑solution matrix with limited intermetallic precipitation, as revealed by electron backscatter diffraction; the relatively low lattice distortion and absence of large, brittle secondary phases translated into a moderate hardness profile that increased progressively with reduced grain size. In contrast, the VZrCr alloy formed a complex network of Zr‑rich intermetallics and Cr‑rich precipitates during rapid solidification, leading to pronounced microsegregation and a higher density of coherent second phases. These features strengthened the alloy but also introduced brittleness, producing a higher average hardness yet a broader distribution of hardness values. Consequently, VZrCr would plausibly trend higher in hardness than ZrHfReTi, primarily due to its richer secondary phase content and associated solid‑solution strengthening.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy HfTaVCr, fabricated by powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS), typically crystallizes in a body‑centred cubic (BCC) solid solution over a wide composition range. During SPS the rapid heating and high pressure promote atomic intermixing, enabling the formation of a single BCC phase that incorporates all five constituent elements into the lattice. The lattice parameters of the resultant alloy lie between the values of pure Hf and V, reflecting a near‑ideal solid‑solution behaviour. Phase stability is governed by a combination of high mixing entropy, which lowers the Gibbs free energy, and the significant atomic size mismatch among Hf, Ta, V, Cr, and C, which produces lattice distortion that further stabilises the BCC structure against formation of competing phases such as hexagonal close‑packed (HCP) or intermetallics. The SPS process also suppresses porosity and promotes homogeneous grain growth, yielding a fine‑grained microstructure that reinforces the solid‑solution strengthening mechanism and enhances the overall mechanical robustness of the alloy.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: phase stability and the formation of BCC solid solutions
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Laser additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloys VHfZrMo and NbReWCrZrMoV produces columnar microstructures with grain sizes ranging from 5 to 15 µm, depending on scanning strategy. In VHfZrMo, the limited number of elements and the presence of a comparatively large Hf atom generate substantial lattice distortion, but the overall solid‑solution strengthening is moderated by the relatively small Mo content and the tendency for V–Zr to form a single BCC solid solution. Consequently, the tensile strength of VHfZrMo is largely governed by its grain‑size‑controlled yield behaviour, with finer grains produced by higher scan speeds yielding modest increases in ultimate tensile strength. By contrast, NbReWCrZrMoV incorporates five transition metals with markedly different atomic radii, leading to pronounced lattice strain and a higher density of coherent precipitates, particularly NbRe–Cr–W intermetallic clusters. These secondary phases act as effective barriers to dislocation motion, and when combined with a fine‑tuned columnar grain size, they produce a more pronounced hardening effect. Thus, NbReWCrZrMoV is expected to trend higher in tensile strength than VHfZrMo, primarily due to stronger solid‑solution and precipitation hardening rather than grain size alone.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: qualitative tensile strength trends relative to composition and grain size

text: In laser additive manufacturing of BCC refractory high‑entropy alloys, the intricate interplay between composition, microstructure, and defect architecture governs notch sensitivity and, consequently, fracture toughness. The VZrTiWMoCrTa alloy, containing six elements with a high atomic‑size mismatch, exhibits pronounced solid‑solution strengthening and a finer columnar grain structure due to the rapid solidification inherent to directed energy deposition. These features elevate the stress‑intensity field required for crack initiation, thereby reducing notch sensitivity and improving fracture toughness relative to more dilute systems. In contrast, ZrVWCr, with only four principal constituents and a comparatively smaller lattice distortion, tends to form coarser grains and may develop elongated pores or melt‑pool defects along the deposition path. The reduced impediment to crack propagation in this alloy leads to a higher notch sensitivity and, thus, lower fracture toughness. Therefore, the six‑element VZrTiWMoCrTa alloy would plausibly trend toward greater notch resistance and superior toughness compared to the four‑element ZrVWCr system.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Arc melting of V, Mo, Ti, Zr, and W was performed under a purified argon atmosphere, with each element weighed to within ±0.1 %. The resulting ingot was flipped and re‑melting four times to ensure compositional uniformity before drop casting into a copper mold to produce a ~2 mm thick plate. Samples were then subjected to a homogenization treatment at 2100 °C for 48 h, followed by furnace cooling to room temperature. This heat treatment reduced residual melt‐segregation by promoting diffusion of the highly mobile elements (V and Zr) into the bulk, leading to a more homogeneous single BCC phase with occasional Zr‑rich secondary precipitates. Transmission electron microscopy revealed a refinement of the grain structure relative to the as‑cast condition, with average grain sizes decreasing from ~70 µm to ~35 µm, and the disappearance of coarse Mo‑rich lamellae. X‑ray diffraction showed a shift of the BCC peaks toward lower 2θ, indicating lattice expansion consistent with increased solid‑solution strengthening. Overall, the homogenized microstructure exhibited a finer, equiaxed grain network and more uniformly distributed lattice distortion, setting the stage for enhanced strength and ductility in subsequent mechanical tests.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Arc melting of the TiCrWMoNbReHf alloy and TiVTa alloy was carried out under an inert argon atmosphere to produce homogeneous ingots, which were subsequently drop‑cast onto a copper hearth to promote rapid solidification. In both cases, the resulting microstructures exhibited a fine equiaxed grain structure with an average grain size of approximately 15–20 µm, as confirmed by optical microscopy. The TiCrWMoNbReHf alloy, containing a broader elemental spectrum, develops significant lattice distortion and higher solid solution strengthening relative to TiVTa. This distortion, coupled with the presence of minor intermetallic precipitates such as Ti₂V and Nb₃Si, tends to increase the yield and ultimate tensile strengths. Conversely, the TiVTa alloy, with a narrower compositional range, displays less lattice strain and fewer secondary phases, leading to a comparatively lower tensile strength but potentially higher ductility due to its more uniform grain refinement. Thus, the TiCrWMoNbReHf alloy is expected to trend higher in tensile strength, while TiVTa may offer superior elongation at fracture.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: qualitative tensile strength trends relative to composition and grain size
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Suction casting of the equiatomic refractory high‑entropy alloy TaVCrHfReTiNb was performed under an argon atmosphere to suppress oxidation and preserve the homogeneous melt. The resulting cast bars exhibited a near‑single β‑phase body‑centered cubic microstructure with fine equiaxed grains (average size ~5 µm) and negligible porosity, as confirmed by optical microscopy and X‑ray tomography. Tensile specimens (gauge length 12 mm, width 6 mm) were tested at room temperature with a 0.01 mm/min strain rate while recording strain from a cross‑head extensometer. Hardness measurements on polished sections revealed a Vickers hardness of 300 HV, which, according to Tabor’s empirical relationship, correlates with a high yield strength. The extensometer data showed an initial linear regime up to ~0.8 % strain, after which a pronounced strain‑hardening plateau was observed, reflecting the interaction between dislocations and the lattice distortion induced by the high atomic number variance. The yield point, defined by the inflection in the stress–strain curve, coincided with the onset of this plateau, confirming that the measured hardness is a reliable proxy for the alloy’s yield strength in this composition.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: the qualitative correlation between hardness and yield strength (Tabor-type reasoning)
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Mechanical alloying of the refractory high‑entropy alloy VHfCrTi, followed by hot‑press sintering, produced a dense polycrystalline material exhibiting a highly distorted bcc lattice and a fine equiaxed grain structure. Extensometer‑based elongation curves acquired during high‑cycle tensile testing revealed a pronounced plateau preceding ultimate failure, indicative of persistent crack nucleation sites. Scanning electron microscopy and EBSD mapping identified preferential crack initiation at grain boundary intersections where residual stress concentrations are amplified by the pronounced lattice distortion introduced by the large atomic size mismatch among V, Hf, Cr, and Ti. During subsequent propagation, the crack path was observed to be highly tortuous, reflecting the heterogeneity of grain orientations and the presence of nanoscale carbides that impede straight‑line growth. The combination of strong solid‑solution strengthening, reduced porosity, and the high density of small precipitates contributed to a delayed crack growth rate, thereby extending fatigue life relative to conventional refractory alloys of comparable composition.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life

text: Mechanical alloying of MoTaTiCrNbZrV powders was conducted in a high‑energy ball mill under argon for 48 h, achieving extensive interdiffusion and a nearly single‑phase BCC solid solution as confirmed by X‑ray diffraction. The milled powders were uniaxially hot‑pressed at 1900 °C and 30 MPa for 30 min, producing fully dense specimens with average grain sizes below 10 µm. Notched tensile tests on Vickers V‑notched bars revealed pronounced sensitivity to stress concentration: the applied notch amplified the local stress state, promoting rapid initiation of brittle cleavage along {110} planes typical of BCC lattices. Microfractographic analysis showed that the fracture surfaces consisted of large, flat facets with minimal plastic deformation, indicative of low fracture toughness. The high lattice distortion from the equiatomic composition, combined with limited ductile phase formation, restricted crack‑tip blunting and therefore heightened notch sensitivity, underscoring the inherent brittleness of this refractory high‑entropy alloy.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: Mechanical alloying of MoZrCrTi and TiVReHfTaCrNb followed by hot‑pressing produced bulk BCC high‑entropy alloys with dense, fine‑grained microstructures. The MoZrCrTi alloy, containing a larger fraction of early transition metals with higher lattice distortion, exhibits a more pronounced grain‑size‑controlled fracture process; its lower average grain size promotes higher fracture toughness by constraining crack advance and enhancing energy dissipation through grain‑boundary sliding. In contrast, TiVReHfTaCrNb possesses a higher overall valence electron concentration and a more extensive presence of refractory elements that stabilize a harder, more brittle BCC lattice, resulting in greater notch sensitivity. The larger atomic size mismatch and reduced dislocation mobility in TiVReHfTaCrNb limit plastic work ahead of a notch, thereby lowering its fracture toughness relative to MoZrCrTi. Thus, notch‑sensitive behaviour and fracture toughness are expected to be higher in the MoZrCrTi alloy, while TiVReHfTaCrNb should show comparatively lower toughness due to its intrinsically brittle BCC microstructure.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: A refractory high entropy alloy comprising V, Nb, Zr, W, Mo, and Hf was synthesized by vacuum induction melting and subsequently homogenized at elevated temperature. The nominal equiatomic composition was examined using electron backscatter diffraction and synchrotron X‑ray diffraction, revealing a predominately body‑centered cubic matrix with fine, dispersed Laves‑phase precipitates and trace intermetallic clusters of the type V2Hf and ZrNbMo. These second‑phase particles nucleate during slow cooling and remain coherent with the matrix at sub‑micrometer scales, providing significant solid‑solution and precipitation strengthening. Grain size measurements indicate a fine‑grained microstructure (<5 µm) that, coupled with the high lattice distortion intrinsic to the six‑component system, results in an elevated yield strength and hardness. The intermetallic network, though continuous at higher cooling rates, is effectively interrupted by the matrix, which mitigates brittle fracture and preserves moderate ductility. Overall, the microstructural features point to a balance of high strength and acceptable fracture toughness suitable for high‑temperature structural applications.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: secondary phase precipitation (Laves phases, intermetallics)

text: Laser additive manufacturing via directed energy deposition was employed to fabricate bulk specimens of the refractory high‑entropy alloys VTiHfReTaZr and HfTaWZrMoNbV. The relative strain‑rate sensitivity of their strength characteristics was evaluated through tensile testing at quasi‑static and high‑strain‑rate conditions. In the VTiHfReTaZr alloy, the combination of a high Ti content and the presence of Re‑rich dendritic microstructures promotes a lower activation energy for dislocation glide, resulting in a modest strain‑rate sensitivity; the alloy’s yield and ultimate strengths increase gradually with increasing strain rate, reflecting a thermally activated deformation mechanism. Conversely, the HfTaWZrMoNbV system contains a significant proportion of high‑melting‑point elements (W, Mo) and displays a finer, more uniformly distributed solid solution strengthening field, which raises the energy barrier for dislocation motion. This leads to a comparatively reduced strain‑rate sensitivity, with strength values that remain nearly constant across the tested strain‑rate window. The disparity can be attributed to the more pronounced lattice distortion and stronger solid‑solution interactions in HfTaWZrMoNbV, which suppress strain‑rate‑induced softening mechanisms that are otherwise more active in VTiHfReTaZr.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: strain rate sensitivity of strength properties

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrCrReNb under an argon atmosphere yields a near‑equiatomic solid solution with a body‑centered cubic lattice and an average lattice parameter that reflects significant lattice distortion from the large Zr atoms and the smaller Cr and Re ions. The resulting microstructure is fine‑grained, with typical grain sizes below 15 µm, and exhibits low porosity due to the rapid solidification inherent to the casting process. However, exposure to ambient humidity or aggressive environments generates surface oxide layers rich in Cr and Zr oxides, which can act as nucleation sites for intergranular cracks, thereby promoting environmental embrittlement. Furthermore, the alloy’s high solubility for hydrogen in the BCC matrix facilitates hydrogen absorption during exposure to hydrogen‑rich atmospheres or during machining. The dissolved hydrogen can partition to grain boundaries, lowering the cohesive energy and encouraging hydrogen‑induced cracking, especially in the presence of the pre‑existing oxide‑coated grain boundaries. Consequently, while the alloy maintains high strength and a low coefficient of thermal expansion, its susceptibility to environmental embrittlement and hydrogen damage must be mitigated through protective coatings or post‑processing heat treatments that reduce residual stress and eliminate hydrogen traps.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: environmental embrittlement and hydrogen effects

text: In comparing the laser‑additive‑manufactured alloys ReNbVCrHfW and TiCrTaVWZr, the dominant contributor to hardness is the nature and quantity of secondary phases that form during rapid solidification. ReNbVCrHfW, rich in refractory transition metals with a high mixing entropy, tends to suppress the formation of large intermetallic precipitates, yielding a more homogeneous solid solution with only fine, coherently‑strained V‑rich or Nb‑rich dispersoids. These sub‑nanometer coherently dispersed particles enhance hardness through Orowan strengthening while preserving ductility. By contrast, TiCrTaVWZr, containing a higher fraction of Zr and Ti, favors the precipitation of brittle, Ti‑rich intermetallics such as TiZr or TiCr phases that nucleate at high density but grow coarser due to slower diffusion in the laser‑fused melt pool. The resulting larger intermetallic particles provide stronger pinning and impede dislocation motion, thereby increasing hardness but at the expense of toughness. Consequently, one would expect TiCrTaVWZr to display a higher hardness than ReNbVCrHfW, primarily because of the greater volume fraction and coarser size of its secondary phase precipitates.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: the effect of secondary phase or precipitate content on hardness

text: Laser additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloy NbTaZrWCr by directed energy deposition was investigated to elucidate how secondary phase evolution influences hardness during high‑temperature service. The melt‑pool dynamics inherent to the process promote rapid solidification, generating a predominantly body‑centered cubic solid solution interspersed with nanoscale intermetallic precipitates composed of (Nb,Ta)W and Zr‑rich carbides. X‑ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy revealed that the volume fraction and spacing of these precipitates are highly sensitive to the build direction and heat‑input parameters; finer spacing and higher precipitate density were achieved with lower laser power and slower travel speeds. Mechanical testing performed in a controlled‑atmosphere furnace up to 1200 °C demonstrated that samples containing the densest precipitate networks exhibited the greatest hardness retention, while those with coarser, less numerous precipitates showed a pronounced decline. The results confirm that maintaining a fine, well‑dispersed secondary phase population during processing is essential for preserving the hardness of NbTaZrWCr under elevated‑temperature loading conditions.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: the effect of secondary phase or precipitate content on hardness

text: A refractory high‑entropy alloy composed of W, Cr, V, Zr, Ti and Nb was fabricated by successive arc‑melting of stoichiometric amounts in a water‑cooled copper hearth under argon, followed by drop‑casting the molten pool into a steel mold to achieve rapid solidification. The resulting cast ingot displayed a single BCC phase with minor lamellar Cr₂Nb intermetallics at grain boundaries. Optical and SEM examinations revealed equiaxed grains of 5–10 µm, considerably finer than the coarse grain structures typical of Ni‑base superalloys produced by directional solidification. Differential scanning calorimetry indicated a broad solidus–liquidus range, suggesting solid‑solution strengthening through extensive lattice distortion inherent to the multi‑principal element system. Mechanical testing at elevated temperatures showed that, unlike Ni‑based alloys which suffer from γ′ phase coarsening above 800 °C, the WCrVZrTiNb alloy maintained its yield strength up to 1100 °C, with only modest softening attributable to reduced grain‑boundary sliding. The absence of γ′ precipitates and the stability of the BCC matrix thus confer a superior high‑temperature strength retention relative to conventional superalloys.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: comparison with conventional Ni-based superalloys in high-temperature contexts

text: In the powder‑metallurgical route to the refractory high‑entropy alloy TaHfWReMoNb, the starting powder mix is compacted and then subjected to spark plasma sintering (SPS) at high temperature and modest pressure, which rapidly densifies the material while limiting overall grain growth. During the brief SPS dwell, the severe plastic deformation imposed by rapid heating and electrical pulse creates a highly distorted lattice and a high density of sub‑grains and dislocations. Upon cooling or during a subsequent annealing step, these stored defects act as driving forces for recrystallization: low‑energy, defect‑free grains nucleate preferentially at sites of high stored energy, such as within the heavily deformed regions or at grain boundaries. Because the alloy contains multiple high‑valence elements with substantial lattice mismatch, the resulting solid‑solution strengthening elevates the critical temperature for nucleation, but once nucleated, the new grains grow rapidly due to the large driving force from the high stored energy. However, the presence of Re, a slow‑diffusing element, introduces a sluggish diffusion effect that constrains the rate of boundary migration, leading to a characteristic two‑stage grain growth behavior: an initial rapid coarsening of the newly formed recrystallites followed by a slower, diffusion‑controlled growth regime. Consequently, the final microstructure after a typical post‑SPS anneal exhibits a fine–to‑moderate grain size that reflects the balance between rapid defect‑driven nucleation, high solid‑solution strain fields, and the diffusion limitations imposed by the refractory constituents.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: recrystallization behavior and grain growth kinetics

text: TaMoHfRe, a refractory high‑entropy alloy composed of transition metals with comparable atomic radii and valence electron concentrations around 4.7, exhibits a near‑equimolar composition that favors the formation of a single solid solution. Mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing enhances atomic intermixing, reducing the Gibbs free energy by increasing configurational entropy and suppressing phase separation. The mixing enthalpy of the constituent pairs is modestly negative (≈ –10 kJ mol⁻¹), which contributes to a slight exothermic tendency yet remains small enough that the high entropy term dominates, stabilizing the body‑centered cubic matrix. Valence electron concentration (VEC) near 4.5–5.0 places the alloy within the transition region between bcc and hcp stability, but the lattice distortion induced by the atomic size mismatch (Δr ≈ 2 %) raises the total free energy sufficiently to lock the bcc phase even at room temperature. Consequently, the thermodynamic landscape of TaMoHfRe promotes a homogeneous, single‑phase solid solution with minimal secondary phases, setting the stage for the mechanical behaviors governed by solid‑solution and grain‑size effects.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: thermodynamic considerations (mixing enthalpy, valence electron concentration)

text: Arc‑melted NbTaCrZrTiVMo alloy was homogenized by drop casting and subsequently evaluated over a broad temperature range. Instrumented indentation revealed a pronounced softening of both hardness and elastic modulus with increasing temperature, with the modulus dropping more rapidly than hardness, indicative of a dominant lattice vibration mechanism. Tensile testing showed that both ultimate and yield strengths decline steadily as the test temperature rises from room temperature to 1200 °C, reflecting the progressive loss of lattice friction strength and the reduction in solid‑solution strengthening contributions from the large atomic‑size mismatch among Nb, Ta, V, and Mo. The high‑temperature yield plateau occurs at a lower stress than expected for a conventional FCC alloy, consistent with the presence of a high density of incoherent nanocrystalline regions that act as early slip sources. Overall, the temperature dependence of the mechanical response can be attributed to the combined effects of lattice thermal softening, grain‑boundary diffusion, and the diminishing efficacy of the severe lattice distortion inherent to this refractory HEA.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: temperature dependence of tensile strength and yield strength

text: Laser directed energy deposition of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrReTiNbWHf produces a rapidly cooled microstructure in which a primary solid solution of the constituent elements is retained with a limited amount of intermetallic secondary phases. The high lattice distortion inherent to this multi‑principal system promotes significant solid‑solution strengthening, but it also creates a network of short‑range compositional fluctuations that can act as preferential pathways for hydrogen uptake. During service in hydrogen‑rich atmospheres, the alloy is susceptible to environmental embrittlement because dissolved hydrogen reduces the cohesive energy at grain boundaries and promotes the nucleation of microvoids and cracks, especially at the coarse precipitates of Re‑rich or Zr‑rich intermetallics that serve as stress concentrators. Moreover, the rapid solidification typical of laser additive manufacturing can trap hydrogen in interstitial sites, leading to localized embrittlement that manifests as a reduction in fracture toughness and an earlier onset of fatigue failure under cyclic loading. Thus, the interplay between the complex solid solution matrix, secondary phase distribution, and hydrogen solubility dictates the susceptibility of ZrReTiNbWHf to environmental embrittlement.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: environmental embrittlement and hydrogen effects

text: Suction casting of TiWNbZrTa and VTiWCr under a controlled argon atmosphere produces coarse‑equiaxed grains with limited porosity, enabling a direct assessment of the Tabor relationship between hardness and yield strength in these refractory high‑entropy alloys. In TiWNbZrTa, the high average atomic size mismatch (≈18 %) promotes pronounced lattice distortion and a pronounced solid‑solution strengthening component, while the presence of Zr and Ta contributes to a finer microstructure through dynamic precipitation of Ti–Zr and Ti–Ta intermetallics during solidification. These features collectively elevate the alloy’s hardness and, by Tabor reasoning, its yield strength. Conversely, VTiWCr, with a lower average atomic radius mismatch (≈12 %) and a higher fraction of vanadium, exhibits a comparatively softer lattice and a tendency for larger, more widely spaced V‑rich precipitates, reducing both hardness and the associated yield strength. Thus, TiWNbZrTa is expected to display a higher hardness–yield strength trend than VTiWCr, primarily due to its greater lattice distortion and finer secondary‑phase distribution.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: the qualitative correlation between hardness and yield strength (Tabor-type reasoning)

text: Powder metallurgy fabrication of the TiVWMoReTaCr high‑entropy alloy involved attrition milling of elemental Ti, V, W, Mo, Re, Ta, and Cr powders followed by cold compaction to 70 % theoretical density, then spark plasma sintering at 1850 °C under 50 MPa for 10 min, yielding near‑full density samples with a single β‑phase body‑centered cubic microstructure. Electron backscatter diffraction revealed a fine, equiaxed grain structure (~1–2 µm) and minor TiC precipitation at grain boundaries. Dynamic mechanical analysis during cyclic loading showed a pronounced increase in the measured Young’s modulus as the applied strain amplitude rose, a trend attributed to the progressive alignment of metallic d‑bond networks and the stiffening effect of Re and W, which enhance the covalent‑metallic bonding character. Fatigue tests at 1 % strain amplitude indicated long life at low cycle counts but a steep reduction beyond 10⁴ cycles, consistent with the modulus rise and the onset of localized cracking along TiC‑rich grain boundaries. The observed correlation between elastic modulus, bonding character, and fatigue behavior underscores the role of compositional tuning in tailoring high‑entropy alloy resilience.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: elastic (Young's) modulus trends and their relation to bonding character and composition

text: Laser additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloy HfNbCrZrVMoW by directed energy deposition produced a columnar‑to‑equiaxed microstructure with average grain widths ranging from 2 µm to 15 µm depending on scan speed. Extensometer‑based tensile testing revealed that specimens fabricated at higher scan speeds, which yielded finer grains, exhibited markedly higher ultimate tensile strength and hardness, consistent with Hall‑Petch predictions: the strengthening contribution scales with the inverse square root of grain diameter, while the grain‑boundary‑controlled deformation resistance increases. In contrast, samples with coarser grains displayed lower peak stresses and a pronounced necking onset at earlier strains, indicating reduced load‑carrying capacity. The measured hardness values paralleled the tensile strength trend, suggesting that grain boundary impediments dominate over solid‑solution effects in this alloy system at the tested conditions. Overall, the data support a strong inverse correlation between grain size and both strength and hardness for HfNbCrZrVMoW fabricated by laser additive manufacturing.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: the relationship between grain size and both strength and hardness (Hall-Petch-type reasoning)

text: Vacuum induction melting of MoNbTiWVRe was carried out in a quartz crucible under a 10‑mTorr argon atmosphere, with a melt time of 30 s and an arc current of 5 kA. Rapid solidification was achieved by quenching onto a water‑cooled copper mold, yielding a microstructure dominated by a primary bcc solid solution. Systematic variation of the Re content (from 5 at.% to 25 at.%) revealed a gradual increase in hardness, consistent with the larger lattice distortion introduced by the heavy Re atom and the concomitant solid solution strengthening. However, at the higher end of the composition range, the appearance of Re‑rich secondary phases (observed as intergranular white bands in optical microscopy) coincided with a plateau in hardness values. These intermetallics, while providing a barrier to dislocation motion, also act as stress concentrators, diminishing the overall increase in hardness that would be expected solely from solid solution effects. Thus, the hardening trend is strongly modulated by the evolution of secondary phase content as a function of Re concentration.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content

text: In a refractory high‑entropy alloy composed of V, W, and Zr (VWZr) produced by vacuum induction melting, the high lattice distortion and limited solubility of Zr in the BCC matrix generate a complex network of interstitially driven dislocations and local misfit strains. These features impede dislocation motion, leading to high yield strength but also render the alloy intrinsically brittle at room temperature. When a notch is introduced, the local stress concentration elevates the stress field near the crack tip, and the lack of ductile phase transformations means that plasticity cannot blunt the crack. Consequently, the fracture toughness is markedly reduced, and notch sensitivity increases sharply. The severity of notch sensitivity correlates with the grain size: finer grains confine the stress field and promote more uniform crack propagation, whereas coarser grains localize stress and accelerate intergranular fracture. Thus, in VWZr, notch sensitivity is a direct manifestation of its BCC microstructure, solid‑solution strengthening, and minimal secondary phase formation, underscoring the delicate balance between strength and toughness in refractory high‑entropy alloys.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: In powder‑metallurgy fabrication of the refractory high‑entropy alloy HfNbTa, the consolidation step by spark‑plasma sintering often leaves residual porosity and micro‑cracks that act as stress concentrators, thereby reducing fracture toughness and accelerating crack initiation during cyclic loading. Nanoindentation mapping reveals that regions of higher local hardness and modulus correlate with the primary solid solution phase, whereas pores and intergranular defects display markedly lower modulus values and increased indentation fracture. The disparity between the stiff, highly distorted lattice of HfNbTa and the compliant voids produces a pronounced heterogeneity in load‑bearing capacity, which in turn promotes crack propagation along the weaker zones. Consequently, fatigue life diminishes because the pores provide preferential paths for crack growth, and the overall fracture toughness is lowered due to the lack of effective toughening mechanisms such as crack bridging or micro‑cracking that would otherwise be present in a fully dense microstructure.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: the effect of porosity or processing defects on fracture toughness and fatigue performance
