text: Vacuum‑induced melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy TaCrHfMoTi produced a dense ingot with minimal porosity, confirmed by optical inspection. The high‑temperature oxidation study, conducted between 1000 °C and 1400 °C in air, revealed a self‑limiting oxidation layer dominated by the formation of a protective chromia‑rich phase. As the temperature rises, the Cr and Ta constituents preferentially segregate to the surface, generating a compact Cr₂O₃ network that impedes oxygen diffusion. Concurrently, Mo and Ti contribute to the stability of the interfacial oxide by forming a mixed MoO₃/TiO₂ layer that adheres strongly to the underlying alloy. The lattice distortion inherent to the multi‑principal system reduces the diffusivity of oxygen through the bulk, further slowing weight gain. When the temperature exceeds 1300 °C, the protective coating begins to spall due to thermal stress, yet the underlying alloy continues to exhibit only modest mass increase, indicating a robust oxidation resistance that stems from the synergistic action of the constituent oxides and the alloy's solid‑solution matrix.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: oxidation behavior at elevated temperature

text: Laser‐directed energy deposition was used to fabricate near‐stoichiometric refractory high‑entropy alloys (HEAs) TaReVNbW and CrZrTiVHfTa, and their tensile response was examined at ambient temperature. Microstructural analysis revealed a columnar dendritic grain structure in both alloys, but TaReVNbW exhibited finer grains and a higher volume fraction of nanoscale coherent carbides, while CrZrTiVHfTa displayed coarser grains and a modest intermetallic network. During deformation, the TaReVNbW alloy demonstrates pronounced work‑hardening, attributable to the high lattice distortion from the wide range of atomic sizes and the impediment of dislocation motion by the dense secondary phase population. In contrast, CrZrTiVHfTa shows a more limited hardening rate, as the larger grains and less pronounced phase contrast allow easier dislocation glide. Consequently, TaReVNbW is expected to trend higher in work‑hardening capacity and maintain elevated flow stress at larger strains compared with CrZrTiVHfTa.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: work hardening behavior during tensile deformation

text: Powder‑metallurgy routes followed by spark‑plasma sintering produced dense monolithic specimens of NbW₀.₇₅Hf₀.₂₅ and CrW₀.₇₅Ta₀.₂₅, each exhibiting a near‑equiatomic composition apart from the minor alloying additions. Microstructural examinations revealed a fine equiaxed grain network for both alloys, yet the CrW₀.₇₅Ta₀.₂₅ matrix contained a higher fraction of secondary W–Cr carbides precipitated during the sintering dwell, whereas the NbW₀.₇₅Hf₀.₂₅ microstructure was dominated by a single solid‑solution phase with slight Nb–Hf partitioning at grain boundaries. The compressive yield stress of CrW₀.₇₅Ta₀.₂₅ exceeded that of NbW₀.₇₅Hf₀.₂₅, a trend attributable to the additional solid‑solution hardening from Ta and the strengthening effect of the carbide inclusions, which impede dislocation glide under compressive loading. In contrast, tensile yield in both alloys displayed a more pronounced asymmetry; the NbW₀.₇₅Hf₀.₂₅ alloy showed a relatively lower tensile yield, likely due to its more uniform lattice distortion and absence of carbides, which reduces the ability of dislocations to nucleate and propagate in tension. Consequently, CrW₀.₇₅Ta₀.₂₅ is projected to exhibit a higher compressive yield strength, while tensile asymmetry favors the NbW₀.₇₅Hf₀.₂₅ alloy to display a lower tensile yield stress
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering

text: In the present study, the refractory high‑entropy alloy CrHfWReNbZrTi was synthesized by high‑energy mechanical alloying followed by hot‑press sintering at 1800 °C under argon, yielding a dense microstructure with sub‑micrometer equiaxed grains and minimal porosity. Oxidation kinetics were evaluated in air from 1200 to 1600 °C for up to 500 h, revealing an initially rapid mass gain that transitions to a parabolic regime. The formation of a continuous Cr‑rich surface oxide layer, enriched in Cr₂O₃, acts as a diffusion barrier for underlying metallic constituents, while the presence of ZrO₂ and HfO₂ precipitates within the bulk contributes to a mixed‑phase protective network that reduces oxygen permeation. The alloy demonstrates superior oxidation resistance compared to binary refractory counterparts, attributable to synergistic lattice distortion and solid‑solution strengthening, which suppress grain boundary diffusion and mitigate scale spallation. These findings suggest that the engineered microstructural features inherent to CrHfWReNbZrTi enhance its high‑temperature oxidative stability, rendering it a promising candidate for structural applications in oxidizing environments.

subtopic: oxidation behavior at elevated temperature

text: Arc melting of the equiatomic mixtures ZrReHfWTi and NbCrTaTiHf was followed by rapid drop casting to produce cast ingots with minimal cooling gradients. Post‑solidification, specimens were machined into notched dog‑bone coupons, with notch radii of 0.5 mm, and subjected to monotonic tensile loading to failure. The BCC framework of both alloys, coupled with high lattice distortion, promotes a high density of twin boundaries that act as barriers to crack propagation. However, the ZrReHfWTi composition incorporates Zr and Ti, which tend to stabilize a more ductile microstructure and increase the propensity for microcrack deflection, thereby reducing notch sensitivity and yielding comparatively higher fracture toughness. In contrast, NbCrTaTiHf contains a higher fraction of Cr and Nb, elements that favor the formation of fine, coherent precipitates that can act as crack initiators, raising notch sensitivity and diminishing fracture toughness. Consequently, the ZrReHfWTi alloy is expected to exhibit a lower notch effect and better fracture resistance than NbCrTaTiHf.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: The vacuum‑induction melted WTaNb alloy, possessing a nearly equiatomic composition, displayed a moderate increase in elongation at fracture relative to its binary counterparts, as inferred from compact‑tension fracture toughness specimens. Fine, equiaxed grains resulting from rapid solidification were observed, and their uniform distribution contributed to a more homogeneous stress field during crack propagation, thereby delaying the onset of micro‑void coalescence. However, the high lattice distortion inherent to the refractory elements produced localized stress concentrators that facilitated the initiation of shear bands at lower applied strains. The presence of minor amorphous intergranular phases, likely formed during cooling, acted as crack‑bridging entities, enhancing energy absorption and permitting additional plastic strain before catastrophic failure. Nonetheless, the relatively coarse precipitates of Ta–W rich intermetallics occasionally served as crack initiation sites, limiting the ultimate ductility. Overall, the interplay between fine grains, lattice distortion, and intergranular features governs the observed balance between elongation at fracture and fracture toughness in this system.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy NbVWReZrHf, fabricated by arc melting and subsequent drop casting, was evaluated for high‑temperature performance relative to conventional Ni‑based superalloys. The multi‑principal composition generates a significant lattice distortion, which impedes dislocation glide and yields a markedly higher yield strength at temperatures above 900 °C compared with Ni‑based alloys that rely primarily on γ′ precipitation for strength. The fine, homogenous microstructure of the drop‑cast material, with grain sizes below 30 µm, reduces the likelihood of creep‑driven grain boundary sliding, leading to a superior creep resistance that remains stable up to 1100 °C. Moreover, the absence of detrimental intermetallic formation and the inherent stability of the body‑centered cubic phase in NbVWReZrHf prevent the loss of strength often observed in Ni‑based superalloys under prolonged thermal exposure. Consequently, this HEA exhibits a more favorable combination of high‑temperature yield strength, elastic modulus, and fracture toughness than its Ni‑based counterparts, positioning it as a promising candidate for next‑generation turbine and power‑generation components.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: comparison with conventional Ni-based superalloys in high-temperature contexts

text: Arc‑melting of equiatomic NbTiMo and VTaReZrMoTi powders was conducted under high‑purity argon, followed by rapid cooling through drop casting into a copper mold to promote a fine equiaxed microstructure. In the NbTiMo alloy, the close atomic size match between Nb, Ti, and Mo yields a nearly lattice‑coherent solid solution, with negligible secondary phase formation. This homogenization, together with a fine grain size (≈10 µm) observed by SEM, facilitates dislocation glide and a relatively high elongation at fracture. By contrast, the VTaReZrMoTi system exhibits pronounced lattice distortion due to the larger size difference between Re and the other elements, leading to the nucleation of small, incoherent intermetallic precipitates during solidification. These precipitates, spaced roughly 200 nm apart, act as obstacles to dislocation motion and serve as sites for stress concentration, thereby reducing ductility. Consequently, the NbTiMo alloy would be expected to display a higher elongation at fracture than VTaReZrMoTi, driven by its more coherent solid solution and finer, less heterogeneous microstructure.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting

text: Suction casting of the refractory BCC high‑entropy alloys MoNbHfWCr and TaTiHf under a controlled argon atmosphere produced dense, near‑equimolar microstructures, yet distinct differences in notch sensitivity emerge from their compositional and structural attributes. In MoNbHfWCr the higher concentration of transition metals with substantial atomic size mismatch induces pronounced lattice distortion, enhancing solid‑solution hardening while simultaneously promoting a finer, more uniform grain network. This grain refinement reduces the likelihood of crack initiation at notches, thereby elevating the fracture toughness relative to the TaTiHf counterpart. Conversely, TaTiHf contains a greater proportion of large‑size elements that tend to form coarse, intermetallic precipitates along grain boundaries; these secondary phases act as stress concentrators and facilitate crack propagation from notches, increasing notch sensitivity. Consequently, the MoNbHfWCr alloy would plausibly exhibit lower notch sensitivity and higher fracture toughness, whereas TaTiHf would trend toward greater notch sensitivity and reduced toughness in their brittle BCC compositions.

text: Laser additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloy VReNbZrTiCr by directed energy deposition yields a complex, multiphase microstructure in which rapid solidification and directional cooling produce pronounced dendritic segregation. Columnar dendrites form along the build direction, with primary arms enriched in high‑melting‑point constituents such as V and Nb, while secondary arms incorporate more refractory Re and Zr. This chemical inhomogeneity generates compositional gradients that are reflected in locally varying lattice parameters and solid solution strengthening. The overall grain size is markedly refined relative to conventional casting, with equiaxed grains of a few hundred micrometers appearing in the interdendritic regions where the local composition is more homogeneous. The combination of dendritic segregation and fine, directionally biased grains enhances resistance to crack initiation, while the presence of minor secondary phases at grain boundaries can impede dislocation motion, contributing to elevated yield strength and hardness in the as‑printed state.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: microstructural features such as dendritic segregation and grain size

text: Powder metallurgy was employed to fabricate bulk TiZrHf specimens, with elemental powders mixed at an equiatomic ratio and milled under argon to promote intimate contact and reduce contamination. The blended powders were compacted to 70 % theoretical density and then subjected to spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1900 °C under a uniaxial pressure of 50 MPa for 5 min, using a heating rate of 100 °C min⁻¹. The rapid heating and short dwell time minimized grain growth, yielding a fine‑grained, nearly single‑phase solid solution dominated by a bcc matrix. During fatigue testing in a closed‑loop servo‑hydraulic machine at room temperature, initial crack nucleation was observed predominantly at grain boundary–phase interfaces, suggesting that local lattice distortion and residual stresses concentrated there. As loading cycles increased, cracks propagated along the plane of maximum shear, with intermittent slowing at high‑angle grain boundaries that acted as barrier sites. The overall fatigue life correlated positively with the fine grain size and the absence of large porosity, while any secondary precipitates or retained oxides accelerated crack growth by serving as stress concentrators.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Suction casting of the refractory high entropy alloy VWZr was conducted in a sealed quartz tube under a continuous flow of high‑purity argon to suppress oxidation of the molten alloy, which possesses a nominal composition of V_25W_25Zr_25Cu_25 (percent by weight). The melt, maintained at 2600 °C, was rapidly drawn through a 1.5 mm diameter nozzle, producing a dense column that was immediately quenched in a liquid nitrogen bath to lock in the high‑temperature solid solution structure and minimize grain growth. Post‑solidification, the surface of the cast rod was subjected to a two‑step coating protocol: first, a thin (≈2 µm) TiN layer was deposited by magnetron sputtering under 5 mTorr nitrogen at 550 °C, providing a barrier to high‑temperature oxidation and enhancing surface hardness; second, a conformal Al₂O₃ film was applied via atomic layer deposition at 300 °C to improve thermal shock resistance. Microstructural analysis revealed that the TiN/Al₂O₃ bilayer adheres to the VWZr matrix through interfacial diffusion of Ti and Al, forming a graded interface that mitigates thermal mismatch stresses during temperature cycling. The coated samples exhibited markedly reduced oxidation rates when exposed to 1200 °C in air, as evidenced by weight‑gain measurements and X‑ray diffraction that showed only minor formation of V₂O₅ and W₃O₈, confirming the efficacy of the dual‑layer strategy for high‑temperature surface protection.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: high-temperature coating or surface protection strategies
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: CrWTa and CrTaTi were synthesized from elemental powders using spark plasma sintering, yielding dense microstructures with similar overall porosity. In both systems the dominant phase is a body‑centered cubic (BCC) matrix, yet CrWTa contains a minor intermetallic TiC‑rich secondary phase that segregates to grain boundaries, whereas CrTaTi exhibits a homogeneous solid solution with only trace amounts of TiC. The TiC precipitates in CrWTa increase local stress concentrations and promote transgranular fracture, reducing the ease with which a crack can be deflected along grain boundaries. Conversely, the absence of pronounced secondary phases in CrTaTi allows for more effective grain‑boundary sliding and the formation of tortuous crack paths, which enhances fracture resistance. Accordingly, CrTaTi is expected to display superior fracture toughness relative to CrWTa, driven by its cleaner grain‑boundary chemistry and higher propensity for crack‑path deflection.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: fracture toughness trends and their relation to phase content, grain boundary character, and crack path

text: Arc‑melted ingots of the refractory HEA ZrHfReCr were repeatedly melted under an argon atmosphere, then drop‑cast into copper molds to promote rapid solidification. Microstructural examination revealed a homogeneous BCC matrix interspersed with nanoscale Laves‑type Zr₂Cr and HfRe precipitates that increased in volume fraction as the Zr:Hf ratio was elevated. Resonant ultrasound spectroscopy (RUS) measured a monotonic rise in the longitudinal elastic modulus with decreasing Zr content, attributable to the higher lattice stiffness of the Re–rich matrix. Hardness mapping showed that specimens with intermediate Zr levels exhibited the greatest microhardness, correlating with an optimal balance between solid‑solution strengthening from the alloying elements and fine precipitate spacing that impedes dislocation motion. In contrast, Zr‑rich compositions, while retaining higher elastic modulus, displayed lower hardness due to coarser precipitates and a reduced degree of lattice distortion. These observations underscore the critical role of secondary phase content and compositional tuning in tailoring the mechanical performance of ZrHfReCr.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Arc‑melting of a stoichiometric TaMoWVZrTi batch was performed under a high‑purity argon atmosphere with a 50 mm water‑cooled copper crucible, ensuring complete homogenization of the refractory elements and minimizing vaporization losses. The resulting ingot was subsequently drop‑cast onto a graphite mold to produce a dense, near‑single‑phase cast alloy. Optical microscopy revealed a lamellar microstructure composed of fine equiaxed grains (average size < 5 µm) interspersed with weakly coherent intermetallic precipitates enriched in W and V. Scanning electron microscopy of fatigue specimens showed crack initiation preferentially at grain boundary junctions where localized stress concentrations are highest; the presence of the secondary W‑rich phases acted to blunt the crack tip, slowing early propagation. Electron backscatter diffraction mapped the lattice distortion around the precipitates, confirming a high degree of solid‑solution strengthening that contributed to a higher threshold stress intensity for crack advance. Moreover, the negligible porosity observed in the as‑cast microstructure reduced extrinsic fatigue damage, leading to a longer fatigue life compared to wrought counterparts with higher defect densities.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Processing the refractory high‑entropy alloy TaHfVMo by vacuum induction melting yields a single‑phase body‑centered cubic microstructure with modest grain refinement. Instrumented indentation tests on this material reveal a pronounced hardness increase relative to its constituent binary alloys, indicating significant solid‑solution strengthening from the large lattice distortion introduced by the disparate atomic radii of Ta, Hf, V, and Mo. However, the same microstructural features that raise hardness also impede dislocation mobility, leading to a reduced elastic modulus as measured by the slope of the unloading curve. This stiffening manifests as a limited capacity for plastic deformation, evidenced by low load‑deformation curves and a narrow plastic region during indentation. Consequently, the alloy displays a classic ductility‑strength trade‑off: as hardness and elastic modulus rise due to the high lattice distortion and potential short‑range ordering, the material’s ability to undergo significant elongation before fracture diminishes, underscoring the need to balance grain size and compositional tuning to optimize both strength and ductility.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: ductility-strength trade-offs (how gains in strength typically come at the cost of elongation)
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Arc‐melting and drop casting produce dense ingots of the refractory high‑entropy alloys NbReWVMoHf and TiWCr, yet their microstructural evolution leads to distinct ductility–strength balances. In NbReWVMoHf, the near‑equimolar combination of large‑size elements (Nb, W, Hf) with smaller Mo and V generates significant lattice distortion and a fine, homogeneous γ‑phase that promotes solid‑solution hardening. The resulting high yield and ultimate tensile strengths are offset by limited slip system activation, yielding reduced elongation to failure. Conversely, TiWCr, containing the smaller Ti atom and a higher proportion of Cr, exhibits a more relaxed lattice parameter mismatch and a dual‑phase microstructure where a minor TiC precipitate is interspersed within a BCC matrix. This arrangement provides moderate strengthening while maintaining a higher number of available slip systems, thereby enhancing ductility relative to NbReWVMoHf. Consequently, TiWCr is expected to show a more favorable strength–ductility trade‑off, achieving comparable strength with greater elongation to fracture.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: ductility-strength trade-offs (how gains in strength typically come at the cost of elongation)

text: In suction casting of TiCrZrTaMo and CrZrTaTiMoReV alloys under argon, microstructural examination revealed contrasting hardness trends attributable to secondary phase chemistry and distribution. The TiCrZrTaMo cast exhibited a largely single BCC solid solution with occasional Ti-rich precipitates, producing a relatively uniform hardness profile and modestly higher hardness relative to the CrZrTaTiMoReV alloy. By contrast, CrZrTaTiMoReV developed a fine network of intermetallic Ti₂Zr and Re-containing intergranular phases that fragmented the microstructure; the presence of these hard, but brittle intermetallics tended to increase peak hardness locally while also inducing porosity at grain boundaries, which in turn lowered overall hardness. Thus, the TiCrZrTaMo alloy is expected to trend higher in bulk hardness due to its simpler phase constitution and lower porosity, whereas CrZrTaTiMoReV shows a broader hardness distribution driven by secondary phase content and intergranular porosity.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: ZrNbTaMo ingots were fabricated by vacuum induction melting with an arc power of 2.5 kW and a melt duration of 15 s per pass, repeated four times to ensure homogeneity. After casting, the ingots were hot‐rolled at 1400 °C to 30 % reduction, followed by solution annealing at 1550 °C for 2 h under argon. Recrystallization was monitored by in situ synchrotron X‑ray diffraction, revealing a shift of the (110) reflection from a broad, heavily strained state to a sharp peak indicative of complete strain relief at 1450 °C. Electron backscatter diffraction maps showed nucleation of equiaxed grains at about 1300 °C, with grain size increasing from an initial 5 µm to ~30 µm by 1500 °C. Grain growth followed a power‑law kinetics (D² ∝ t) with a growth exponent of 0.6, suggesting that lattice distortion and limited diffusion of Zr in the high‑entropy matrix retard growth relative to conventional refractory alloys. The resulting microstructure exhibited a uniform grain distribution and low porosity, which are expected to influence the alloy’s high‑temperature mechanical performance.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: recrystallization behavior and grain growth kinetics
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering produced a dense VTaReHfWCr alloy whose microstructure is dominated by a fine network of secondary precipitates. During the rapid sintering step the high solute concentration and substantial lattice distortion of the solid solution drive the precipitation of Laves‑type phases, notably (V,Cr)₂W and (Ta,Re)Hf₂, which nucleate heterogeneously at grain boundaries and along dislocation cores. The Laves phases form at relatively low volume fractions yet create a highly non‑equiaxed morphology that impedes dislocation motion through Orowan bowing. Concurrently, minor intermetallics such as Ta₃Cr and V₆Hf precipitate as coherent islands within the matrix, contributing additional solid‑solution and precipitation hardening. The combined effect of these second phases is a substantial increase in yield strength and hardness while the grain boundary network retains sufficient ductility, as the fine precipitates act as obstacles without severely compromising strain‑tolerance. The resulting microstructure thus balances strength and toughness through controlled secondary phase precipitation.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: secondary phase precipitation (Laves phases, intermetallics)

text: Suction casting of WZrCr and ZrNbMoV was carried out in a quartz crucible under an argon atmosphere to suppress oxidation. Both alloys were cast at 1700 °C and immediately quenched in liquid nitrogen, producing a fine-grained microstructure with a near-equiatomic lattice and limited secondary phase formation. Electron backscatter diffraction revealed that the WZrCr matrix exhibits a higher lattice distortion due to the larger atomic size mismatch between W and Cr, while the ZrNbMoV alloy shows a more homogeneous solid solution with a lower overall strain field. Hardness measurements performed on polished cross‑sections indicated that WZrCr is consistently harder than ZrNbMoV, which is consistent with the Tabor relation linking hardness to yield strength: the greater lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening in WZrCr should translate into a higher yield stress. Accordingly, tensile tests displayed a higher yield point for WZrCr, corroborating the hardness trend and suggesting that the increased resistance to dislocation motion in the W‑rich matrix dominates the mechanical response.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: the qualitative correlation between hardness and yield strength (Tabor-type reasoning)
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Laser additive manufacturing via directed energy deposition was employed to fabricate cylindrical test specimens of two refractory high‑entropy alloys: TaCrReHfMoW (Ta‑Cr‑Re‑Hf‑Mo‑W) and TiWHfZrTaMo (Ti‑W‑Hf‑Zr‑Ta‑Mo). Process parameters were matched to yield comparable melt‑pool geometries and minimal macro‑porosity, but the TiWHfZrTaMo build exhibited a higher degree of columnar grain growth along the deposition direction due to the larger lattice mismatch among Ti, W, and Hf. In high‑cycle fatigue tests at room temperature, crack initiation in TaCrReHfMoW preferentially occurred at sites of residual compressive stress accumulation associated with finer equiaxed grains and a more homogeneous distribution of solid solution strengthening, leading to a slower propagation rate governed by frequent micro‑crack deflection. Conversely, TiWHfZrTaMo showed early initiation along the columnar grain boundaries where the Ti–W–Hf network facilitates localized slip and a higher propensity for micro‑void coalescence. Consequently, the fatigue life of TaCrReHfMoW is plausibly higher than that of TiWHfZrTaMo, driven by its finer grain structure, lower porosity, and more uniform solid‑solution strengthening field that impede crack nucleation and reduce the effective crack‑growth velocity.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy WTiZr in an inert argon atmosphere yielded a dense, nearly single‑phase microstructure dominated by a BCC matrix. Vickers microhardness measurements performed at 10 distinct sites revealed a consistent hardening trend that correlates strongly with the expected solid‑solution strengthening contribution of the alloy’s constituent elements. The high lattice distortion imposed by the atomic size mismatch among W, Ti, and Zr atoms produces a pronounced resistance to dislocation glide, reflected in the elevated hardness values relative to binary W–Zr or W–Ti alloys. Spatial variations in hardness, albeit modest, mirror subtle compositional inhomogeneities introduced during the rapid solidification inherent to suction casting, which locally alter the effective solute concentration and thus the magnitude of solid‑solution strengthening. Consequently, the observed yield strength of WTiZr, inferred from the hardness data via the conventional conversion relationship, is markedly higher than that of its binary counterparts, underscoring the pivotal role of multi‑element lattice distortion in enhancing mechanical performance.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: qualitative yield strength trends and their relation to solid solution strengthening

text: The suction‑cast ReVWTi alloy, fabricated under a purified argon atmosphere to suppress oxygen pickup, displays a near‑equimolar elemental distribution and a body‑centered cubic (BCC) matrix with trace intermetallic precipitates. Initial as‑cast microstructure shows a fine, irregular grain network with an average size below 5 µm, typical of rapid solidification. During post‑cast annealing at 1200 °C, recrystallization initiates along pre‑existing high‑energy grain boundaries, leading to a gradual development of equiaxed grains. The recrystallized grain size expands to 20–30 µm after 1 h, with the growth rate diminishing sharply thereafter due to lattice distortion imposed by the large atomic radius mismatch among Re, V, W, and Ti. The high vacancy concentration at elevated temperature facilitates rapid nucleation, while the substantial solid‑solution strengthening from Re and W limits grain boundary mobility, yielding a modest growth exponent. Consequently, the alloy achieves a stable grain size plateau, which is expected to correlate with enhanced yield strength and fatigue resistance while preserving ductility through the retained fine secondary precipitates.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: recrystallization behavior and grain growth kinetics

text: CrReTiVHfNb is a representative refractory high‑entropy alloy whose composition comprises five elements from the transition metal series (Cr, Re, Ti, V, Hf, Nb) that are known to favor a body‑centered cubic (BCC) lattice at high temperatures. When processed by vacuum induction melting, the rapid solidification and high‑purity environment suppress oxidation and promote homogeneous mixing of the constituent atoms. The large atomic size mismatch among the components induces lattice distortion, which raises the configurational entropy and stabilizes the BCC solid solution against the formation of intermetallics. Thermodynamic calculations based on the CALPHAD approach show that the Gibbs free energy of mixing remains negative across the entire temperature range of interest, confirming the thermodynamic favorability of the single‑phase BCC structure. The resulting microstructure is characterized by a fine, equiaxed grain structure with minimal segregation, which in turn supports uniform mechanical behavior. This intrinsic stability of the BCC solid solution is a key factor that underlies the high-temperature strength and resistance to grain growth observed in CrReTiVHfNb alloys.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: phase stability and the formation of BCC solid solutions
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: A V‑Hf‑Ta‑Nb alloy was fabricated by vacuum induction melting of the constituent elements in stoichiometric proportions, followed by water‑quench casting and homogenization at 1800 °C for 12 h. The resultant ingot was machined into dog‑bone specimens (gauge length 12 mm, width 4 mm) for uniaxial tensile testing, and into compact‑tension (CT) coupons (50 mm × 15 mm) for fracture‑toughness measurements. During tensile deformation, a pronounced work‑hardening plateau was observed after initial elastic strain; the hardening rate decreased gradually, indicative of dynamic strain‑age mechanisms. CT fracture surfaces revealed transgranular cracking with numerous fine slip bands radiating from the crack tip, suggesting that grain refinement and solid‑solution strengthening from the high lattice distortion in V and Hf dominate the toughening response. The work‑hardening trend correlated with an increase in K_IC values compared to a coarse‑grained counterpart, underscoring the role of microstructural fine‑scale deformation in enhancing fracture resistance.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: work hardening behavior during tensile deformation
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Laser‐directed energy deposition of the refractory high‑entropy alloy VReTiWCr yields a dense microstructure dominated by a body‑centered cubic (BCC) matrix with a high fraction of fine equiaxed grains. Rockwell hardness measurements across a temperature range of 25 °C to 800 °C reveal a pronounced decrease in hardness with increasing temperature, reflecting thermally activated dislocation glide and reduced lattice friction. Correspondingly, tensile tests performed at 25 °C, 400 °C, and 700 °C indicate a monotonic decline in both ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and yield strength (YS) as temperature rises. The temperature‑dependent hardening trend can be attributed to the diminishing effectiveness of solid‑solution strengthening from the high lattice distortion inherent in VReTiWCr, coupled with increased recovery and recrystallization activity at elevated temperatures. These observations highlight the critical role of temperature‑induced microstructural evolution in governing the mechanical response of this refractory HEA and underscore the necessity of controlling grain refinement and phase stability during additive manufacturing to preserve strength at elevated service temperatures.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: temperature dependence of tensile strength and yield strength

text: Both MoVTaReCrNb and VWTaCrZrReMo were synthesized by arc melting and subsequent drop casting, yielding coarse columnar grains with minor porosity. The MoVTaReCrNb composition, which contains a higher proportion of the early transition metals Mo and V, shows a relatively finer, more equiaxed grain structure due to a reduced solidification range, promoting dislocation activity and slip system activation. In contrast, VWTaCrZrReMo incorporates Zr, a larger atomic radius, which induces significant lattice distortion and forms a network of fine intermetallic precipitates during solidification, constraining grain growth but also creating obstacles to dislocation motion. Consequently, MoVTaReCrNb exhibits greater elongation at fracture, as the finer grains facilitate strain partitioning and reduce stress concentrators. The VWTaCrZrReMo alloy, while potentially offering higher strength from solid‑solution and precipitation hardening, tends toward lower ductility because the precipitate network and larger lattice distortion limit slip and promote early cracking.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: Laser‑directed energy deposition was employed to fabricate near‑equiatomic NbZrVHfMoTa, yielding a dense columnar microstructure with sub‑micron primary grains and secondary Ti‑free β‑phase lamellae. Nanoindentation mapping revealed a pronounced correlation between grain size and mechanical response: finer equiaxed grains exhibited local hardness values up to 1.8 times that of coarser columnar regions, while the reduced elastic modulus displayed a subtler, yet consistent, increase. The Hall‑Petch relation was evident as the inverse square root dependence of hardness on grain diameter, consistent with dislocation pile‑up limiting mechanisms within the BCC lattice. Variations in compositional segregation at grain boundaries, particularly Nb enrichment, were shown to enhance local hardness via solid‑solution strengthening. Additionally, the lamellar β‑phase acted as a second phase that impeded dislocation motion, contributing to an overall rise in hardness and strength in the fine‑grained zones. This study underscores the critical role of grain refinement in tuning the strength–hardness landscape of refractory high‑entropy alloys.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: the relationship between grain size and both strength and hardness (Hall-Petch-type reasoning)

text: The TiWZrReCrTa alloy, fabricated by suction casting in an inert argon atmosphere, exhibits a pronounced microstructural heterogeneity that directly informs its elastic response. Nanoindentation mapping reveals two distinct modulus bands: a high‑modulus phase (~300 GPa) correlating with Ti‑rich, BCC‑like matrix regions where strong covalent bonding dominates, and a comparatively lower‑modulus band (~250 GPa) associated with W‑ and Re‑rich sub‑domains that display increased metallic character and lattice distortion. The elevated modulus in Ti‑rich zones reflects the short Ti–Ti and Ti–Zr interatomic distances, promoting stiff bonding networks, while the presence of heavy Re and W atoms expands the lattice, reduces bond strength, and introduces significant lattice strain that lowers the effective modulus. Local hardness maps mirror this trend, with higher hardness values co‑located with the stiffer Ti‑rich phase, confirming that bonding character and compositional partitioning are the principal drivers of elastic property variation in this refractory high‑entropy alloy.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: elastic (Young's) modulus trends and their relation to bonding character and composition

text: Mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing yields a fully dense CrTaTiRe high‑entropy alloy in which the constituent elements are atomically mixed within a BCC solid solution. Subsequent annealing at elevated temperatures (600–800 °C) induces pronounced microstructural evolution: coarsening of sub‑nanometer lattice distortions, annihilation of high‑density defects introduced during ball milling, and the emergence of a weakly ordered secondary phase enriched in Cr and Re. The homogenization process reduces compositional segregation, resulting in a more uniform lattice parameter across the sample and a concomitant decrease in lattice strain. Grain growth occurs gradually, producing a bimodal distribution that balances the hardening contribution of fine grains with the ductility imparted by larger grains. As the annealing duration increases, the secondary phase precipitates become more widely spaced, lowering the frequency of strain‑induced decohesion sites and thereby enhancing elongation at fracture while slightly reducing hardness. Overall, controlled annealing optimizes the trade‑off between strength and ductility through tailored grain size, solid‑solution uniformity, and precipitate spacing.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure

text: In the refractory high‑entropy alloy CrReMoHf, the coexistence of five elements with markedly different metallic radii introduces substantial lattice distortion that dominates its mechanical behavior. Cr and Mo possess relatively small atomic sizes, whereas Hf and Re are considerably larger, creating a broad distribution of interatomic distances within the solid solution. During powder‑metallurgy fabrication and subsequent spark‑plasma sintering, this size mismatch promotes the formation of a highly strained, body‑centered cubic (BCC) matrix that resists dislocation glide through enhanced solid‑solution hardening. The distorted lattice also hampers the nucleation of slip planes, contributing to a higher yield strength and hardness relative to conventional alloys of similar composition. Moreover, the severe lattice distortion elevates the activation energy for diffusion, suppressing grain growth during sintering and thus maintaining a fine‑grained microstructure that further elevates strength. The combination of these effects explains the observed trend of increased strength with higher atomic size disparity in CrReMoHf, while preserving relatively good ductility through the retention of BCC slip systems.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: lattice distortion effects from atomic size mismatch
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: The TiZrMoReCr alloy, synthesized through high‑energy ball milling and subsequent hot‑press sintering, exhibits a predominantly BCC lattice with minor Ti‑rich Laves phases that localize at grain boundaries. Mechanical alloying generates an ultrafine grain size in the 0.5–1 µm range, which, coupled with solid solution strengthening from the large atomic size mismatch of Re and Cr, elevates the yield strength. The high fraction of equiaxed grains, preserved by rapid consolidation, limits the propensity for grain‑boundary sliding, thereby retaining a moderate ductile response. However, the presence of nanoscale secondary Ti₂Zr and Mo-rich precipitates introduces local stress concentrations that serve as initiation sites for shear band nucleation, curtailing elongation at fracture. Furthermore, any residual porosity, arising from incomplete densification during hot pressing, exacerbates crack propagation. Consequently, the alloy shows respectable tensile ductility relative to single‑phase refractory HEAs but remains bounded by the competition between refined grain‑size‑driven toughness and precipitate‑induced brittleness.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: Laser additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ReVNb was performed using directed‑energy deposition on a pre‑oxidized Nb‑substrate. A 1.8 kW YAG laser scanned in a raster pattern at 12 mm s⁻¹ with a 0.2 mm spot size yielded a dense, columnar‑grained microstructure, confirmed by SEM back‑scattered imaging and EDS mapping which showed a near‑equiatomic distribution of Re, V, and Nb. X‑ray diffraction revealed a single bcc phase with a lattice parameter slightly larger than that of pure Nb, indicating significant lattice distortion. Compared to Ni‑base superalloys, ReVNb displayed markedly higher creep resistance at 1200 °C, attributed to the sluggish diffusion of the heavy Re atoms and the strong solid‑solution strengthening from V and Nb. The absence of γ′ precipitates in ReVNb leads to a more uniform stress distribution, while the higher density of high‑angle grain boundaries promotes stable grain growth without significant intergranular cracking, contrasting with the typical grain‑boundary embrittlement observed in Ni‑superalloys under similar thermal cycling.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: comparison with conventional Ni-based superalloys in high-temperature contexts
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: In the refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrReMoVNbCrW, vacuum induction melting provides a homogeneous melt that quickly quenches to lock in a single‑phase body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution. The constituent elements—zirconium, rhenium, molybdenum, vanadium, niobium, chromium, and tungsten—span a broad range of atomic radii and electronegativities, generating substantial lattice distortion. This distortion raises the configurational entropy, which stabilizes the BCC phase over competing hexagonal close‑packed or ordered intermetallic structures at room temperature. During solidification, the high cooling rate suppresses diffusion‑driven phase separation, preventing the formation of intermetallic precipitates such as ReMo or NbCr phases that would otherwise nucleate at high temperatures. The resulting single‑phase BCC matrix exhibits a random distribution of the seven elements, with no detectable secondary phases in X‑ray diffraction patterns, confirming the alloy’s phase stability. The BCC lattice accommodates solid‑solution strengthening from both size mismatch and modulus differences among the constituent atoms, contributing to the alloy’s overall mechanical robustness.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: phase stability and the formation of BCC solid solutions
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ReZrTaVCrWNb under a high‑purity argon atmosphere produces a dense, fine‑grained microstructure dominated by a BCC solid solution with minor intermetallic precipitates of Re‑rich and Cr‑rich phases. The severe rapid solidification inherent to the process imposes a high cooling rate that refines the primary grain size to a few micrometres, thereby amplifying lattice‑distortion and solid‑solution strengthening contributions from the large atomic‑size mismatch among Re, Zr, Ta, V, Cr, W, and Nb. In compression, the yield stress rises markedly compared to tension because of the higher resistance to dislocation nucleation and glide imposed by the dense, high‑angle grain boundaries that impede slip plane activation more effectively under compressive loads. Additionally, the presence of fine Re‑rich precipitates provides a forest of obstacles that preferentially impede the motion of partials in compression, further elevating the compressive yield point. Consequently, the alloy exhibits a pronounced yield asymmetry: compressive yield strength surpasses tensile yield by a significant margin, while both retain high ductility due to the retained grain‑boundary‑mediated deformation mechanisms and the absence of critical porosity.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy VZrMo yields a single‑phase bcc microstructure with pronounced dendritic segregation arising from the disparate atomic mobilities of V, Zr, and Mo during solidification. The primary dendritic arm spacing averages 50–70 µm, while interdendritic regions exhibit a finer lamellar spacing of 10–15 µm, reflecting rapid local solidification and reduced undercooling. Post‑solidification homogenization at 1900 °C for 30 min markedly reduces the compositional contrast, yet residual Zr enrichment persists in interdendritic zones, creating localized lattice distortion that contributes to solid‑solution strengthening. Grain size measurements reveal equiaxed grains of 80–120 µm, with a slight tendency towards columnar growth along the temperature gradient imposed by the melting apparatus. The interplay between dendritic segregation and grain refinement suggests that the alloy’s mechanical performance will be governed by a balance of intragranular solid‑solution hardening and intergranular resistance to dislocation motion, offering a pathway to tailor strength and ductility through controlled thermal processing.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: microstructural features such as dendritic segregation and grain size

text: In both directed‐energy deposition builds, the CrTaHfVWReTi and WHfNbTiCrV specimens were fabricated under identical laser power, scan speed, and powder feed rates to ensure comparable thermal histories. Post‐processing involved solution treatment at 1700 °C followed by rapid quenching, producing a predominantly BCC solid solution with minor secondary Ti‐rich carbides. Mechanical testing at 25 °C, 500 °C, and 800 °C revealed distinct strain‑rate sensitivities: the CrTaHfVWReTi alloy, with its higher Hf content and resultant larger lattice distortion, exhibited a pronounced increase in flow stress with decreasing strain rate, indicative of significant solid‑solution strengthening and a propensity for rate‑dependent dislocation glide. Conversely, WHfNbTiCrV, possessing a higher Nb/Ti ratio and a more uniform grain size distribution, displayed a comparatively flat stress–strain curve across strain rates, suggesting lower activation energy for dislocation motion and reduced strain‑rate sensitivity. These trends reflect the underlying differences in solute‐atom scattering and the stability of secondary carbide phases between the two high‑entropy systems.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: strain rate sensitivity of strength properties
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: In comparing the refractory high‑entropy alloys ZrWTiTaHf and TaWVNbHfCr processed identically by arc melting and drop casting, the primary determinant of elongation at fracture is the stability and distribution of the body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution versus any secondary precipitates or phase separation that occur during rapid solidification. ZrWTiTaHf, with a larger lattice parameter mismatch among its constituent elements and a higher fraction of interstitial Ti, tends to retain a more homogeneous BCC matrix; its lower propensity for the formation of hard, brittle intermetallics allows grain boundary sliding and dislocation motion to accommodate strain, yielding relatively higher ductility. Conversely, TaWVNbHfCr contains a significant amount of V, which promotes the nucleation of coherent, high‑strength Nb–Cr rich precipitates during solidification. These coherent second phases impede dislocation glide and restrict grain boundary mobility, leading to a more brittle response and reduced elongation. Thus, ZrWTiTaHf would plausibly exhibit greater elongation at fracture than TaWVNbHfCr due to its more uniform microstructure and diminished secondary‑phase strengthening that otherwise limits ductility.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: The TaTiWReZrHfNb alloy, cast by suction under argon, develops a predominantly body‑centred cubic matrix with a subtle, composition‑driven dendritic network. Rapid solidification suppresses extensive elemental partitioning; however, the higher lattice distortion associated with W and Ta drives a measurable segregation of Re and Zr toward the dendrite cores, generating a fine secondary phase of Re‑rich intermetallics that act as localized hardening sites. Grain size averages 20–30 µm, but the dendritic structure imposes a bimodal distribution where interdendritic regions exhibit coarser grains (≈40 µm) while dendrite arms remain refined (≈15 µm). This heterogeneity enhances overall strength by combining fine‑grain Hall–Petch strengthening in the arms with solid‑solution hardening from the lattice distortion of the multi‑principal elements. The presence of minor porosity (<0.5 vol %) near the casting surface slightly lowers ductility but does not significantly perturb the tensile behaviour of the bulk material.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: microstructural features such as dendritic segregation and grain size

text: In this study, the refractory high‑entropy alloy NbTaCrMoHfZr was fabricated by laser‑directed energy deposition and subjected to systematic Vickers microhardness mapping to infer fracture‑toughness behavior. Across multiple indentation sites, hardness exhibited a bimodal distribution correlated with the presence of a primary solid solution matrix and secondary, carbided intermetallic networks. Indentations that intercepted coherent Cr‑rich intermetallic precipitates produced localized hardening and a pronounced crack‑deflection response, indicative of a toughening mechanism driven by the increased grain‑boundary character at precipitate–matrix interfaces. In contrast, regions dominated by the high‑entropy solid solution displayed smoother crack propagation paths and lower hardness, reflecting fewer microstructural obstacles to crack advance. The observed trend suggests that maximizing interfacial grain‑boundary area and promoting stable intermetallic phase formation can enhance fracture toughness by providing effective crack‑blocking sites, while excessive solid‑solution hardening without sufficient phase dispersion may lead to brittle failure.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: fracture toughness trends and their relation to phase content, grain boundary character, and crack path

text: In a comparative assessment of the powder‐metallurgy and spark plasma sintered refractory high entropy alloys WCrHf and WHfTaTiCrMo, the influence of lattice distortion and secondary phase evolution on the ductility–strength interplay is evident. The WCrHf system, with a relatively low number of constituent elements and a moderate Burgers vector mismatch, develops a dense network of sub‑micron carbides that precipitate during sintering. These precipitates impede dislocation glide, producing a pronounced solid‑solution strengthening effect that elevates yield and ultimate strength while simultaneously constraining the capacity for plastic strain, resulting in a modest elongation at fracture. Conversely, WHfTaTiCrMo incorporates five principal elements, generating a higher degree of lattice parameter spread that intrinsically increases solid‑solution hardening. However, the broader distribution of Ta and Ti promotes the formation of a fine, homogenous β‑phase matrix with limited carbide segregation, preserving a more uniform dislocation activity and enabling a comparatively higher ductility at a given strength level. Thus, while both alloys exhibit strength gains linked to microstructural refinement, WCrHf is expected to trend toward a higher strength–lower elongation combination, whereas WHfTaTiCrMo should retain greater elongation for similar strength metrics.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: ductility-strength trade-offs (how gains in strength typically come at the cost of elongation)

text: Laser additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloys MoTiZrV and VMoWReNbHfZr by directed energy deposition reveals distinct anisotropy in tensile response that correlates with their microstructural evolution under rapid solidification. The MoTiZrV build exhibits a pronounced columnar grain structure aligned with the melt‑pool direction, leading to enhanced tensile strength along the build axis while the transverse strength is modestly reduced due to strain‑induced texture and reduced intergranular cohesion. In contrast, the multi‑component VMoWReNbHfZr alloy develops a more equiaxed microstructure with fine secondary precipitates of Nb–W–Re rich intermetallics, which homogenize load transfer and mitigate anisotropy; tensile properties are comparatively isotropic, with only a slight drop in strength along the build direction attributed to residual porosity. Thus, MoTiZrV is likely to display higher axial strength but lower transverse performance, whereas VMoWReNbHfZr offers more uniform behavior due to its finer, more homogeneous microstructure.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples

text: Suction casting of ReHfMo and CrVTaHfWMoZr under an argon atmosphere yields coarse equiaxed microstructures with limited segregation, yet the two systems diverge markedly in their tensile strength trends. ReHfMo, a tri‑element alloy, exhibits a smaller lattice parameter mismatch and thus lower lattice distortion, which translates into a modest solid‑solution strengthening contribution. Its relatively fine grain refinement during rapid solidification also contributes to a higher yield and ultimate tensile strength compared to coarse‑grained counterparts. In contrast, CrVTaHfWMoZr is a seven‑element high‑entropy solid solution that imposes significant lattice distortion and a more pronounced solid‑solution effect, but its broader compositional spread promotes the formation of fine, coherent secondary phases such as (Cr,V)Ta and (Hf,Zr)Mo precipitates that can impede dislocation motion. However, the same high distortion also raises the propensity for localized strain hardening and potential grain boundary weakening at high temperatures. Overall, the multicomponent alloy is expected to show a higher tensile strength at ambient conditions due to its combined solid‑solution and precipitation hardening, but may exhibit a slightly lower strength-to-weight ratio because of the heavier Re content in ReHfMo.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: qualitative tensile strength trends relative to composition and grain size

text: During suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrReHfW, a 50‑mm diameter ingot was formed under a 1‑atm argon atmosphere to suppress oxidation of the reactive Zr and Hf constituents. The rapid solidification rate of ~10⁵ K s⁻¹ produced a dendritic microstructure with primary dendrite arm spacings of 12–15 µm. Subsequent grinding and polishing revealed a network of sub‑micron pores, predominantly located along interdendritic regions where the Re‑rich liquid solidified last. Rockwell hardness measurements, carried out at H2 load, indicated a mean hardness of 520 HRB with a standard deviation of ±25 HRB, while localized hardness dips correlated strongly with porosity clusters. These voids act as stress concentrators during cyclic loading, reducing fracture toughness by promoting crack initiation at the pore tips and limiting crack‑closure mechanisms. Fatigue tests performed to 10⁶ cycles at 1 % strain amplitude revealed a reduction in life by approximately 30 % compared to cast samples with <0.1 vol % porosity, underscoring the sensitivity of ZrReHfW to processing‑induced defects.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: the effect of porosity or processing defects on fracture toughness and fatigue performance
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Laser‐directed energy deposition was employed to fabricate the refractory high‐entropy alloy TaZrVNbMoW, whose thermodynamic landscape is governed by a largely negative mixing enthalpy and a valence electron concentration (VEC) near 4.1. First‑principles calculations reveal that the constituent elements, all possessing bcc‑stable phases at elevated temperatures, interact through significant atomic size mismatch and electronic contributions that favor an energetically homogeneous solid solution over intermetallic segregation. The calculated mixing enthalpy, largely negative, indicates strong miscibility and predicts the formation of a single β‑phase upon rapid solidification, while the VEC suggests a high‐density of states at the Fermi level that stabilizes the bcc lattice. Thermal analysis during laser processing demonstrates a narrow solidification interval that suppresses the appearance of competing Laves or sigma phases. Consequently, the alloy’s thermodynamic profile supports the attainment of a uniform microstructure, which is anticipated to translate into robust mechanical performance across the high‐temperature regime.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: thermodynamic considerations (mixing enthalpy, valence electron concentration)

text: This study compares the elastic behavior of two refractory high‑entropy alloys, TaHfZrMoRe and TaMoReWTiNb, fabricated by powder metallurgy followed by spark‑plasma sintering. Both systems exhibit a body‑centred cubic lattice, but the former incorporates the early transition metal Zr and the late transition metal Hf, which possess larger atomic radii and relatively weaker covalent‑metallic bonding. Consequently, the average bond strength in TaHfZrMoRe is modest, leading to a lower Young’s modulus relative to the latter alloy. In TaMoReWTiNb, the presence of Mo and Nb—elements with higher electron densities and more compact lattices—enhances the overall metallic‑bond character, while the addition of W, a high‑modulus element, further stiffens the lattice. The combination of strong metallic bonding and reduced lattice distortion in TaMoReWTiNb therefore predicts a higher elastic modulus, whereas TaHfZrMoRe is expected to display a comparatively softer elastic response.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: elastic (Young's) modulus trends and their relation to bonding character and composition

text: Both ReVCrZrTa and WTaHfCr were fabricated by arc melting and subsequent drop casting, yielding equimolar BCC structures with minimal porosity. In these brittle high‑entropy systems, notch sensitivity is governed by the competition between lattice distortion, secondary phase distribution, and the propensity for crack‑tip plasticity. ReVCrZrTa, containing the lighter refractory Re and V, exhibits a larger lattice strain field and a finer grain size due to rapid solidification, which enhances strain‑gradient hardening and reduces crack‑tip opening. Consequently, this alloy displays lower notch sensitivity and a higher apparent fracture toughness compared to WTaHfCr. In contrast, WTaHfCr contains heavier W and Hf atoms, producing a higher degree of atomic size mismatch but also promoting the formation of coarse, brittle Hf‑rich secondary phases that act as crack initiation sites. The reduced plasticity ahead of the notch and increased stress concentration in WTaHfCr lead to a steeper stress‑corrosion response and a comparatively lower fracture toughness. Thus, ReVCrZrTa is expected to trend toward greater notch tolerance and improved resistance to crack propagation in BCC high‑entropy alloys.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy VMoReZrWTiCr, fabricated through powder metallurgy followed by spark‑plasma sintering, exhibits a pronounced asymmetry between its tensile and compressive yield responses that is directly linked to its microstructure. During sintering, a nearly equiatomic mixture of elemental powders develops a fine, body‑centered cubic matrix with dispersed nano‑scale secondary phases such as (Mo,Re)Ti rich precipitates and a minor fraction of V‑rich carbides. Grain refinement to sub‑micron dimensions and the high lattice distortion intrinsic to the multicomponent system collectively enhance solid‑solution strengthening, raising the yield strength in both loading modes. However, under compression, the material benefits additionally from the ability of the matrix to undergo twinning and the secondary phases to impede dislocation pile‑ups, leading to a higher compressive yield stress compared to the tensile case. Three‑point bend fracture toughness tests conducted per ASTM E399/E1820 reveal a toughness plateau that is maintained over a range of strain rates, confirming that the combined effects of fine grains, high solid‑solution contribution, and the presence of coherent precipitates provide a robust barrier against crack initiation while still allowing plastic accommodation under compressive loading.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: In the refractory high‑entropy alloy NbWTaVZrTiMo, the mechanical alloying step generates a chemically homogeneous solid solution with a body‑centred cubic lattice, while the subsequent hot‑pressing consolidates the powder into a dense monolithic structure with a fine, sub‑micron grain population. The extreme lattice distortion introduced by the large atomic size mismatch among Nb, W, Ta, V, Zr, Ti, and Mo atoms promotes extensive solid‑solution strengthening, which raises both the yield strength and hardness. Empirically, hardness measured by micro‑indentation correlates strongly with yield strength according to the Tabor relationship: the indentation depth is inversely related to the elastic response, so harder alloys typically exhibit higher resistance to plastic deformation. In this HEA, the fine grain size further amplifies hardness via the Hall‑Petch effect, while simultaneously elevating yield strength; thus, a higher hardness directly implies a higher yield strength, reflecting the shared dependence on grain boundary strengthening and lattice distortion.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: the qualitative correlation between hardness and yield strength (Tabor-type reasoning)
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Laser additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloy TaMoHf by directed energy deposition produces a dense, equiatomic microstructure with minimal porosity. The Vickers microhardness measurements performed over a grid of indentations reveal a systematic increase in hardness from the substrate through the melt‑pool rim to the fully solidified top layer, reflecting the evolution of local chemistry and texture. Regions closer to the melt‑pool boundary exhibit slightly lower hardness values, consistent with a higher fraction of solid solution‑strengthened Ta–Mo solid solutions, while the fully consolidated zones contain a more uniform distribution of Ta, Mo, and Hf, leading to higher hardness due to increased lattice distortion and stronger covalent bonding contributions. The observed hardness variation correlates with elastic modulus changes inferred from load‑displacement curves, where areas with higher Ta–Hf content display a higher Young’s modulus. This trend supports the notion that the increased d‑band overlap and enhanced metallic bonding in Ta‑rich environments elevate the modulus, whereas Mo‑rich regions, with more metallic character, yield relatively lower stiffness. Thus, the measured Vickers hardness maps serve as a proxy for local modulus variations, highlighting the strong dependence of elastic behavior on compositional homogeneity and bonding character in TaMoHf fabricated by laser additive manufacturing.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: elastic (Young's) modulus trends and their relation to bonding character and composition

text: Samples of NbCrMoTaZr were fabricated by arc melting a stoichiometric mixture of high‑purity elements under an argon atmosphere, followed by a rapid drop‑casting step into a copper mold to promote high cooling rates. The as‑cast ingots were homogenized by a brief anneal at 1700 °C to reduce residual porosity and ensure chemical uniformity. Optical and SEM observations revealed a dense microstructure with fine, equiaxed grains of average size ~5 µm, indicative of the rapid solidification inherent to drop casting. The high lattice distortion introduced by the large atomic size mismatch among Nb, Cr, Mo, Ta, and Zr acts as a potent source of solid solution strengthening: the alloy exhibits a markedly elevated yield strength relative to binary counterparts. Moreover, the observed absence of secondary phase precipitates implies that the strengthening derives predominantly from the dislocation–solvent interaction, with the Cr and Zr content enhancing the resistance to dislocation motion. Thus, the processing route successfully promotes a high solid‑solution strengthened microstructure with superior yield resistance.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: qualitative yield strength trends and their relation to solid solution strengthening
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Arc‑melted ZrTaCrVTi and NbMoW were fabricated by drop casting into copper molds to achieve dense, single‑phase body‑centered cubic (BCC) microstructures. Microstructural examination revealed that ZrTaCrVTi possessed a finer, equiaxed grain network (~10 µm) compared with the coarser (~30 µm) grains of NbMoW, reflecting the higher thermal diffusivity of the former’s constituent elements. Grain‑boundary cohesion in the Ti‑rich ZrTaCrVTi alloy promotes crack deflection, thereby reducing notch sensitivity and enhancing fracture toughness relative to NbMoW, where larger grains and lower lattice distortion facilitate easier crack initiation at notches. Solid‑solution strengthening in both alloys arises from substantial lattice parameter mismatches; however, the higher average atomic radius in ZrTaCrVTi induces greater lattice distortion, further impeding dislocation motion and contributing to a more resilient fracture response. Consequently, ZrTaCrVTi is expected to exhibit lower notch sensitivity and higher fracture toughness than NbMoW, despite both retaining brittle BCC character at room temperature.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: Laser additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloy WMoReTaTiNb by directed energy deposition yields a microstructure dominated by a solid solution matrix with dispersed Laves‑type secondary phases. Across the composition spectrum examined, the relative fraction of the (W,Mo)₂(Re,Ta) intermetallic phase rises with increasing Re content while Ti and Nb reduce its volume fraction. As the intermetallic content increases, hardness shows a monotonic rise due to the hard, brittle nature of the Laves phase, which impedes dislocation motion. Conversely, samples with higher Ti and Nb fractions exhibit a lower secondary phase volume, resulting in a softer matrix and lower hardness. Grain refinement produced by the rapid solidification inherent to laser deposition further accentuates the hardening effect in alloys with higher intermetallic content, whereas coarser grains in Ti‑rich compositions lead to a relative drop in hardness. Thus, the qualitative trend indicates that enhancing intermetallic phase content through compositional tuning directly translates into increased hardness in WMoReTaTiNb alloys.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content

text: Suction casting of the two refractory high‑entropy alloys, ZrReTaTiV and WNbHfCrMoTiZr, produces dense, fine‑grained microstructures but the elemental contrasts give rise to distinct hardening pathways. In ZrReTaTiV, the relatively low lattice distortion and moderate solid‑solution hardening are compensated by the formation of a modest amount of intermetallic precipitates such as (Zr,Ti)₃V and Re-rich intermetallics that nucleate at the grain boundaries. These precipitates, while increasing hardness, also act as stress concentrators, limiting the overall strengthening effect. Conversely, the WNbHfCrMoTiZr alloy experiences a much larger lattice mismatch because of the wide range of atomic radii, leading to pronounced solid‑solution strengthening. Additionally, its propensity to form fine, coherent secondary phases such as W–Ti carbides or (Nb,Mo)₂Ti intermetallics distributed throughout the matrix further impedes dislocation motion. The higher density of such coherent precipitates, combined with the significant lattice distortion, typically drives the hardness of WNbHfCrMoTiZr above that of ZrReTaTiV, even though both alloys are cast under similar inert conditions.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy VHfTi, synthesized by powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS), typically exhibits a body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with a coarse, equiaxed grain structure imposed by the rapid sintering cycle. Subsequent annealing or homogenization at elevated temperatures is employed to relieve residual stresses, promote solute diffusion, and reduce short‑range compositional fluctuations. During this heat treatment, Hf and Ti atoms gradually redistribute, diminishing local lattice distortions and allowing the BCC lattice to approach a more uniform solid solution state. Grain growth can occur, but controlled cooling rates prevent excessive coarsening. The homogenized microstructure features fewer internal boundaries and reduced porosity, which in turn lowers the probability of crack initiation sites. Consequently, the alloy gains enhanced ductility and fatigue resistance, while the uniform lattice strengthens the material against localized deformation and reduces the tendency for intergranular failure.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Arc melting and subsequent drop casting were employed to synthesize two refractory high‑entropy alloys, ZrHfTa and CrMoW, allowing a direct comparison of their microstructural evolution and resulting yield strength behaviors. In ZrHfTa, the lattice parameter is relatively large and the constituent elements exhibit a pronounced size mismatch, promoting a high degree of lattice distortion that acts as an effective solid‑solution strengthening mechanism; this distortion hampers dislocation motion and is expected to elevate the yield stress relative to CrMoW. By contrast, CrMoW consists of transition metals with smaller atomic radii and a more compact bcc lattice; although solid‑solution strengthening still contributes, the smaller size mismatch yields a less pronounced lattice distortion, allowing dislocations to glide more easily and leading to a comparatively lower yield strength. Thus, the ZrHfTa alloy is anticipated to display a higher yield strength, driven primarily by its greater lattice distortion and consequent solid‑solution hardening.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: qualitative yield strength trends and their relation to solid solution strengthening

text: Arc-melted ingots of the refractory HEAs TaTiMoZr and ReTaZrTiNb were homogenized by a series of remelts and then drop cast into a preheated copper mold to achieve rapid solidification. Optical microscopy revealed that the TaTiMoZr microstructure consists of a nearly single-phase bcc solid solution with equiaxed grains averaging 15 µm, while the ReTaZrTiNb alloy exhibited a finer, dendritic network with a mean grain size around 8 µm and isolated Re-rich intermetallic precipitates. Microhardness testing on polished cross sections indicated a higher Vickers hardness for ReTaZrTiNb, consistent with the greater lattice distortion introduced by Re and the presence of secondary precipitates that impede dislocation motion. According to Tabor’s proportionality between hardness and yield strength, the ReTaZrTiNb alloy is expected to display a correspondingly higher yield strength. The coarser grains and lower solute strengthening in TaTiMoZr explain its relatively softer, lower-yielding response.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: the qualitative correlation between hardness and yield strength (Tabor-type reasoning)
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: In the present study, the refractory high‑entropy alloy TiHfReZrTa was synthesized by high‑energy mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing, yielding a near‑equiatomic solid solution with a body‑centered cubic lattice. Microstructural examination revealed a refined grain size of ~10 µm and a low volume fraction of nanoscale Ti–Zr rich precipitates, both of which contribute to an enhanced uniform elongation during tensile deformation. The alloy exhibits a gradual strain‑hardening response before the onset of necking, indicating effective dislocation storage and limited dynamic recrystallization. Cyclic fatigue tests carried out at a stress amplitude of 0.4 σ_y showed a fatigue life that scales inversely with the number of load cycles, with a pronounced change in slope at ~10^5 cycles attributable to the initiation of microcracks along grain boundary faceting. Post‑fatigue fractography revealed a mixture of transgranular and intergranular cracking, the latter being mitigated by the coherent Ti–Zr precipitates that act as crack‑deflection sites. Overall, the fine grain size, low porosity, and coherent secondary phases synergistically enhance elongation at fracture while defining a fatigue‑life regime governed by grain‑boundary interactions and precipitate‑induced crack arrest.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: Vacuum‑induction–melted samples of the ternary refractory high‑entropy alloy TaMoW and the complex 7‑component system VReMoCrHfTaTi were evaluated for strain‑rate dependent strength. The markedly larger lattice distortion and higher configurational entropy in VReMoCrHfTaTi promote stronger solid‑solution hardening, yet the coexistence of multiple refractory elements also introduces a wider distribution of local modulus and activation volume, which can enhance the sensitivity of dislocation glide to imposed strain rates. In contrast, TaMoW, with a more limited elemental spectrum and a comparatively homogeneous solid solution, displays a more sluggish response of its yield strength to rate changes, reflecting a lower activation volume for dislocation motion.
